speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 59, I wish to move a motion to refer to committees the supplementary estimates which have just been tabled by my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). It is a long motion which basically refers to the various standing committees the same type of items that were referred to the standing committees in connection with the main estimates. There is one exception, and that is that no items are referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs because that committee is overloaded. Estimates which might have been referred to that standing committee are referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. I would ask if the motion could be considered as if read. It is in the hands of the leaders of the various parties.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) for his statement, and I thank the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) for tabling this latest illustration of the practice by this government of the art of restraint amounting to further expenditures totalling $1.9 billion. I wonder if the government House leader would consider a departure from accepted practice, that is, dealing with supplementary estimates first and bringing in the main estimates at the end. That might be a more acceptable and far more informative way of proceeding.
It really is fascinating. We go from 1973-74 with a total of $20 billion, to 1974-75 with a total of $27 billion, some 17 per cent increase-no, Mr. Speaker, it will be far more than that. I was contemplating that even this government, acting at its best, would have kept these supplementary estimates down to some $600 million, but the President of the Treasury Board says this is it. It is $1,917 billion. No matter how you slice it, that is the total amount. That would then be some $27 billion, and if you relate that to the 1975-76 main estimates of $28 billion with a comparable increase, you are looking at a total of some $36 billion or $37 billion for a total of the main estimates of-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I tabled the estimates without making any comment. If the hon. member wants me to comment, I will have something to say. The procedure is that when we table the estimates, no comments are made. If the hon. member wants me to reply to him, I will be delighted to give him the details, but that is something that should be done in committee.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) raises an interesting point of order. The supplementary estimates were tabled by him without comment. That, of course, precluded the possibility of comment by opposition parties on the estimates themselves. However, the President of the Treasury Board was followed by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) who simply moved the referral, but in so doing he made a brief comment about the business of the House and the allotment of opposition days. I think that opens up some commentary about the scheduling of business of that nature. However, in fairness, that commentary ought not to be directed toward the substance of the estimates, but to the business of the House. The President of the Treasury Board is absolutely right, no statement was made about the substance of the estimates. Something was said by the President of the Privy Council about the business of the House, and perhaps any comment should be confined to that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I appreciate the point, Mr. Speaker. I can understand why the President of the Treasury Board would not want to make any comment about these estimates.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What I had to say was just preliminary to the proposition by the President of the Privy Council in recommending an innovation, which we accept, that the estimates be sent to the standing committees which are related to the particular items in question. That is a very good idea. It is particularly necessary because of the size and complexity of these supplementary estimates. That is the only reason I was making the comment.
You are out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I can, without being out of order, use a comment made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when the main 1975-76 estimates were tabled. He spoke about the price of civilization; I have to say, "by gosh, the price isn't right here." The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), like Horatius at the bridge, restraining his impetuous colleagues in their desire to spend money worked wonders.
We will facilitate the passage of this motion. It is an excellent idea to get these estimates into the hands of the committees so they can do a better job. It is about time we did something to minimize the farce which takes place in this parliament in connection with the examination of estimates. This is not a partisan issue; there are feelings on the other side of the House too. I know the President of the Privy Council agrees with me, as does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. A proposal has now been made before the committee on procedure which would allow members of the House, in their capacity as members of the committee of the whole, an opportunity to make a meaningful examination of the estimates. I hope not too many days will elapse before this proposition becomes part of the interim orders which will be proposed to this House.

Mr. Speaker, the supplementary estimates were tabled without any statement being made, so it is not in order to make a statement in response to a non-statement. It is also clear that the motion to refer the estimates to the various standing committees is made under Standing Order 59 which, similarly, permits no debate. However, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) did make a brief statement having to do with the business of the House, so perhaps I might comment briefly on that aspect.
We welcome the fact that the estimates are going to the same committees as the main estimates and we are pleased that the minister has now given us information as to which days in the balance of this semester will be opposition days. As the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has pointed out, it is common knowledge that discussions are taking place regarding a change in our supply procedure, at least on a trial basis. One of the advantages of the change we shall probably make is that it would keep the government on notice-it will not know which of the departments will be called back to the House for examina-

tion here either in place of or in addition to the examination in committee. We shall do our part in the committees. We shall do our part here on the floor, as well.

Mr. Speaker, in a few words I should like to say that I am very pleased to see, not only that nature is awakening but that winter is finally coming to an end. From the motions introduced today by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), I see that the government has also come out of its sleep and really wants Parliament to work very arduously during the month of March.
A while ago, it was announced that there would be seven opposition days before the Easter break, and that in addition we would study supplementary estimates (D). Copy of it was just handed to me. I have not had a chance to even thumb through it. I see that several departments are concerned in these estimates. We will have the opportunity of studying them. In any event, I trust that we will not limit ourselves to the figures but that we will look in depth at the legislation so that the people can benefit from the advantages expected from these supplementary estimates as well as from other budgets previously introduced in this House.
For our part, we will co-operate wholeheartedly so that the business of the House can make quick progress, and we can give the people the impression not only that we want to manage the country seriously, but also that we want to do it in all honesty, and as efficiently and quickly as possible.

speechtext:
1.	With reference to Triangle Pacific Forest Products Ltd., in Slocan, British Columbia, has this lumber mill ever received a DREE grant for a salvage mill and, if so (a) for how much (b) on what date was the grant awarded (c) how many new jobs were to be created under this grant?

speechtext:

answer for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is as follows: 1. Yes: (a) The grant offered was for $127,779 and represented 15% of the new capital costs of the total project; (b) The offer of assistance was accepted by Triangle Pacific Forest Products Ltd. on July 4, 1972 for the expansion of their Slocan, British Columbia operations, which in part (approximately 38 per cent was related to a salvage mill; (c) The estimated number of on-site jobs which would be created by the expansion was 64.

As the final payments on such assistance cannot be before 36 months or after 42 months of the commencement of commercial production, and as the amount of assistance on jobs is based on the average number of jobs, or the average wage bill, during years two and three after the commencement of commercial production, some control is maintained over the new employment during this period.

speechtext:
1.	What was the cause of the accident near Bridgetown, Nova Scotia on November 30 in which a militia vehicle was demolished and seven soldiers sent to hospital?
2.	What is the condition of the seven soldiers at this time?
3.	How old and of what type were the tires on the vehicle?
4.	How old was the vehicle and had it received proper safety inspections prior to the accident?
5.	How many tires were purchased for military vehicles during each year 1966 to 1974 to date?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE, ACCIDENT, BRIDGETOWN, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:

Has CIDA re-allocated in the present fiscal year a sum of $117 million and, if so, what was the purpose of the re-allocation and for what specific projects and purposes will the re-allocation sums be spent?

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, CIDA, as a matter of normal practice, adjusts its spending patterns to reflect changing priorities in the recipient countries and patterns of availability of certain goods and services in Canada which are to be supplied to those developing countries. The $117 million in readjustments were a response to the increased and urgent needs of many developing countries caused by the energy crisis, inflationary factors and shortages of food grains. Projects such as the purchase of rice seedlings, financing of hydro electric and the purchase of fertilizer, etc. were advanced. Seven projects which were already under way, in the amount of $20.1 million, were advanced. In addition, ten projects were considered for early approval to help in off-setting the effects of energy costs and inflation, in the amount of $24.9 million. Finally, at the World Food Conference in Rome, last November, Canada pledged $50 million in food aid to the countries in greatest need. It was considered that six countries were on the priority list for this assistance. This amount of $50 million ($51.4 million to be exact) was in addition to the $20 million previously allocated to Bangladesh, one of the most seriously affected
March 3, 1975

countries, making a total food aid commitment of $71.4 million in addition to the original regular allocation for the 1974-75 fiscal year. These allocations represent $116.4 million in development assistance and food aid.

Mr. Speaker, I rarely intrude upon the time of the House in respect of matters of procedure or order, but I am deeply disturbed in reference to question No. 39 which was placed on the order paper on September 30. It is identical to one placed on the order paper during the preceding parliament, on April 8, 1974, and it deals with the sale of munitions by this country to various parts of the world. In light of reports as to vast sales to Viet Nam and to Turkey, and the article in Maclean's which suggests that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is strongly pro-Turkey on the Cypriot question, I am wondering why there is no way this parliament can find out why this great peacekeeping country of the world, so we are told, sells so many munitions all over the world that it takes a year for the figures to be toted up.
I hope there is nothing worse than ministerial misfeasance here. I believe this is a very serious question affecting the stature of Canada in the international community and I am anxious to have an answer as soon as possible, as, I think, are the people of Canada.

Oral Questions
explanation. Hear, hear!

speechtext: Since in this Parliament we are giving increased recognition to the position of women in society, I think it is suitable that the Solicitor General should be there on this occasion. I ask the Minister of Finance whether it is still his position that the alternative to some sort of national consensus on income and inflation restraint is that there will be a period of "prolonged and bitter industrial strife which could leave everyone considerably worse off by substantially reducing the size of the pie that is available to be shared between us". Is that still the position?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL DISLOCATION THROUGH STRIKES- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SOLVE

longed and bitter industrial strife, what does he propose to do?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the problems this country now faces, of course, which is recognized by those in charge of the various aspects of the economy including leaders of labour, is the fact that labour settlements in Canada in the last quarter of 1974 were running at roughly double the rate of settlements in the United States, jeopardizing our competitive position. Because of our situation, those on all sides of the economy recognize that a consensus is necessary. That is why we have had far from discouraging results in the conversations we have had.

LEVEL OF PRICE INCREASES FOR NEXT TWO YEARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in light of that observation, I wonder whether the minister accepts the proposition that inflation and the expectations of continuing high inflation are at the heart of the industrial problems which lie ahead of us. subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Acting Prime Minister regarding the hearings on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline which are taking place today in Yellowknife before the Berger commission. In view of the fact that Mr. Justice Berger has been authorized by the government to consider the social, environmental and economic impact of the proposed Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline and to recommend the terms and conditions which should be imposed on any successful applicant, I ask the Acting Prime Minister the following question: can he assure the House that no authorization to proceed with the project will be granted until the government has received and examined the report of the Berger commission?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I could not give such a categorical assurance. It would depend a great deal on the nature of the report to be presented by Mr. Justice Berger.

subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Acting Prime Minister misunderstood my question. I was not asking whether the government would agree not to proceed if Mr. Justice Berger's report should be negative. But in view of the fact that the government appointed Mr. Justice Berger to look into the social, environmental and economic aspects of this measure, will the minister undertake to assure the House and the people of Canada that the government will not proceed with the construction of the Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline until it has received the report of the commission which the government itself set up for the purpose of looking into this question?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would hesitate to give a categorical reply to this question. It is our hope that Mr. Justice Berger will bring down his report in time for it to be considered when we receive a recommendation from the National Energy Board. If it should be a recommendation to proceed with the building of the pipeline, I could imagine circumstances under which it might be desirable to have some consultations with Mr. Justice Berger about the nature of his report, if it appeared that the time he was going to take would be so long as to interfere with what was considered to be a very desirable decision.

subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the National Energy Board will be looking into the engineering aspects and the supply and demand question, but not into the social, envi-
March 3, 1975

ronmental and economic aspects, I ask the Acting Prime Minister whether this means that the government has already made up its mind, as was indicated by the President of the Treasury Board who when Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said at Yellowknife on January 18 that, "this government, after carefully weighing all the factors involved, has come to the conclusion that a gas pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley is in the national interest." Are we to take it from that statement that the government has already decided to act, and that all the other assurances are a sop to the general public in order to pacify the opposition, and the government intends to go ahead without waiting for the Berger report or any other relevant data?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-EFFECT ON ENVIRONMENT-REQUEST PROJECT NOT PROCEED UNTIL RECEIPT OF BERGER REPORT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, that is not the conclusion one should draw. I think there is a general understanding of urgency in respect of a decision because of the energy situation and the need to know whether in fact there will be access to gas from the Arctic. I believe there is general agreement, also, that the social and environmental factors should be looked at very carefully. From long experience I would rather hesitate to say which of these particular steps must come first in such a process. It is an extremely complicated one. I believe that the government is looking at all aspects of the problem carefully and with all the attention that I think the problem requires. But I would hesitate to say that one particular step has to be completed before a decision can be made, because it might be in the public interest at that time to adopt a somewhat different procedure in order to reach the right decision.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING AGENCY FOR POULTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture.
In view of the fact that poultry producers from the St. Damase Co-op in Quebec have, in protest, intercepted an American truck loaded with United States imported chickens, while their own production quotas have been reduced, can the minister advise the House whether the National Farm Products Marketing Council has received an application for the creation of a national marketing agency for poultry and, if so, whether this application will be granted?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING AGENCY FOR POULTRY
speechtext:
As I have said in the House on many occasions, poultry production is not under a national marketing agency. Public hearings were held last year on whether such a national marketing agency should be established. After the meetings were held, a consensus was reached that they should proceed with negotiations for setting up a national agency for broilers, but this has not been done, mainly because of the controversy in which CEMA was involved at that time. I have no intention of proceeding with it at this time unless
Oral Questions
we have more federal authority for a national marketing board than we have for CEMA at present, which makes it unworkable in my opinion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING AGENCY FOR POULTRY
speechtext: A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Could the minister tell the House whether Canada must now resort to poultry imports, since Canadian production is deficient, in order to meet the internal market needs?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING AGENCY FOR POULTRY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. There is a great deal of poultry in Canada at present, not as much as there was last year at this time but sufficient to supply the Canadian market. Until procedures are developed for what we call supply management on a national basis, there is not much one can do about imports so long as they are not being dumped in this country.

subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION IN BERGER COMMISSION HEARINGS
speechtext: My question is supplementary to a previous question and it is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. It has to do with a previous question with regard to the Berger commission. subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION IN BERGER COMMISSION HEARINGS
speechtext: I appreciate the answer of the Acting Prime Minister. subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION IN BERGER COMMISSION HEARINGS
speechtext:

taxpayers, and are therefore entitled to the expertise and knowledge already developed within the Department of the Environment so that they might better judge the situation and present a better brief to the commission.

subsubtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION IN BERGER COMMISSION HEARINGS

I certainly have a particular interest in the motion to appoint a special committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to consider the green paper on immigration policy. I look forward to following its deliberations and receiving a report from such a committee on a matter which I consider to be of extreme importance.
The conclusions of the committee will be of great assistance in formulating a comprehensive review of policies and programs in the immigration field. The general process of review was embarked upon, when the green paper was tabled on February 3, or even earlier, a year or so ago, when we discussed the possibility that such a green paper might be forthcoming.
As I have said in the House on other occasions, the green paper does not itself make definite recommendations nor does it propose cut and dried solutions to the questions set out therein. Rather, it explores the issues of immigration and population growth, and discusses some of the choices which are open to us. It is a document Canadians may use when considering these or other options in relation to Canada's population future. The green paper is presented as a means of assisting the process of policy formulation and the examination of the new legislation which the government intends to submit to parliament soon. Accordingly, it has been made public in the hope that it will stimulate a country-wide debate upon immigration policy. I might add that this hope or intention appears to be on the way to fulfilment since the green paper was tabled a month ago.
Immigration Green Paper
It is also my hope that the debate will not only embrace such questions as selection procedures and administrative control, in other words, the nuts and bolts of immigration machinery, but that it should also take into consideration the development of a population policy for Canada to which immigration is closely linked.
There is a need to develop a common idea with regard to population growth in Canada and to be clear about its goals if all regions of Canada are to realize their full economic and social potential, avoiding the concentration of too many people in some areas and the presence of an insufficient number of people in others.
I know there are some who say that, because of the sheer physical size of our country and the relatively high standard of living our people enjoy, the population question is an academic one. On the other hand, there is a great deal of concern about the consequences of increasing urbanization, the many problems which accompany that process and which make the question of population growth one of urgent importance right now. At the same time there are other considerations. Alberta may need more workers, while the maritime provinces might be more concerned about internal migration.
There have been a host of world developments, including the population explosion. I am told that the world population is increasing at the rate of some 200,000 people a day. Then again there is the threat of food shortages, both now and in the future. All these events have made us appreciate much more the importance of knowing where we are going in population terms, of making deliberate rather than benign decisions.
While the green paper concentrates mainly on immigration policy, it is also concerned with demographic policy and population policy. We note that immigration based on current trends, of which we are aware, is very likely if those trends continue to replace natural increase as the main source of population growth in this country before the end of the century. Therefore, a sound immigration policy for the future will need to rest squarely on the foundation of some views, and some policy flowing from those views, on population in this country.
If we are to examine population policy and immigration in that context, we must be just as concerned with where people live in Canada as about how many people there are here. We must also recognize that immigration itself is not the only factor. Perhaps quantitatively it will not be the main factor because of the consequence of internal migration trends in this country. So population policies, in short, must deal with the question of distribution as much as with the question of growth. In this regard there is an obviously inherent question for Canadians in the prairie and Atlantic regions.
As I have indicated in my comments, the federal government has begun to study the various aspects of the demographic question and has concluded that we need guidelines for the future. We hope that these guidelines will provide the framework within which to integrate a whole array of interrelated policy measures and ideas affecting population trends, a spectrum of policies that will cover areas such as regional development, urban objectives, na-

March 3, 1975
Immigration Green Paper
tional characteristics, as well as transportation, communications and industrial growth.
We must also recognize in this process that some of the decisions and policies are the responsibility of one level of government. In other areas of endeavour, responsibility and jurisdiction lie between governments or with both the federal and provincial governments. Some are purely provincial and some, in my opinion, in this context, require the input of the municipalities.
It is also our conviction that the formulation and broad acceptance of an over-all set of population goals are very important if the various related policies that are carried out by all these levels of government, plus the private sector, are to yield the maximum results. In this sense the federal government is beginning to foster the widest possible measure of agreement about Canada's population future, and I outlined the consultative machinery when I tabled the green paper in early February.
Speaking of the green paper, Mr. Speaker, I think this is the first time that the government has tried to tell the whole immigration story in detail, and within a really comprehensive framework. It is also the first time that immigration policy has been discussed in relation to these wider economic, demographic, social and cultural concerns. The committee will, of course, be in charge of its own affairs within the terms of reference agreed upon by this House, but I believe that during its work and travels it will provide an extremely valuable stimulus for public debate and, most important, will be the major forum in which Canadians, whether as individuals or through representative organizations, can take part in a debate that will lead to an important decision regarding the future of this country.
I hope that when this joint committee hears Canadians presenting points of view, the variety of hopes and needs of people in all regions of Canada can be related to our decisions about immigration and, in the broader sense, population. In short, I see the committee acting as the paramount vehicle for the recording and transmission of the public's views to the government. In addition to the members of the House and from the other place who will play an active role in the work of the committee, I trust all members of parliament will have a vital role in what I hope will be a constructive national debate on this whole question.
I think the review upon which we have embarked provides a rather unique opportunity for parliamentarians to study all aspects of immigration and to contribute to the best kind of immigration policy that our joint efforts can produce when this debate is concluded. In that context I have already noted, with very considerable appreciation as a matter of fact, that many members of parliament have begun a lively, informed and productive debate among their constituents. Indeed, I am getting many requests from individual members for assistance in providing factual material, and in some cases logistical help.
One has only to pick up a newspaper, or to turn on a television set or radio to realize that the green paper debate is already under way. Generally speaking, the reaction I have had or heard about has been reasonably constructive. Obviously there are some-this is only to be anticipated-who criticize the green paper or question the

government's reason for producing such a document. Having had some experience in this field now, I might say that we should all be concerned about extremist reactions from whatever direction they may come. I have said in this chamber before, as well as said publicly elsewhere, and I repeat it again now, that I believe Canadians will want an immigration policy which has universally applied selection criteria, a policy that is free from discrimination on the basis of race, colour or creed.
If I may go on to try to put this in its proper light, it is false to say that we are flashing a red light on immigration. It has been suggested that Canada might be wise no longer to consider uncontrolled immigration in terms of numbers, that there should be a re-examination of Canada's population future. I do not think anyone is saying that we should do anything less than at least manage the flow of immigrants. By embarking upon this examination quite openly and in public, it is not my intention to slam the door. It is not a red light but perhaps a caution light when the suggestion is made that we should proceed from here forward with more policy consideration than perhaps we had heretofore.
I think that the scope, importance and magnitude of the issues involved in the green paper demand very thoughtful and mature participation on the part of all Canadians. We will all be following closely the activities and deliberations of the special joint committee. This chamber of course will have another significant opportunity to examine immigration policy when, if all goes well, I present a draft bill to parliament in the fall for referral to the appropriate standing committee. I am quite sure that at that stage there will be an opportunity for very intensive scrutiny. That is suggested and planned. I look forward to the completion of this procees with the passage of a new Immigration Act and the accompanying regulations taking place not too far into 1976.
I would hope that the Immigration Act will be sufficiently flexible to accommodate whatever future population policy might emerge after the intensive federal-provincial consultations to which I earlier referred, but in that sense I really do not believe we can afford to wait for these longer term policies before dealing with immigration legislation. Certainly in my view it is essential that our immigration laws be brought up to date as soon as possible, particularly if we are to cope with changing world conditions and if we are to have a legislative framework within which to manage better our own immigration programs.
I appreciate the opportunity of leading off this debate. I look forward to the remarks of hon. members opposite, and to the House giving its approval so that we can get on with the deliberations in the committee on this very important matter.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought after you put the motion that we were playing musical chairs like, "After you, Alphonse," to settle who was going to be first. I thought an agreement had been reached prior to calling the motion that the minister would lead off with a short statement on his views on how the committee first
March 3, 1975

of all should be struck and what its major functions should be.
It is my intention today, on behalf of the party of which I am a member, to place before the House some of our views on the approach we feel the committee should take, and in respect of some of the questions that we feel must be discussed by the committee. I should also like to point out the manner in which we think these discussions should take place.
Since the motion to create a joint committee was tabled on February 24 we have been very much aware of certain provisions within it which we believe need explanation and clarification. This committee which many of us have been waiting for some time to begin its work, is now to undertake this function. There are certain concerns I should like to place on the record.
On February 3 the minister tabled the green paper, at which time this party called for the creation of a select parliamentary committee to study that document and the questions which flowed from it. I am pleased the minister has seen fit to accept that suggestion by formalizing it into the motion we have before us at this time.
It has been and remains our concern that the main estimates tabled by the government should be studied in detail, just as the estimates of any other department, by the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, regardless of the work to be done by the select committee. We thought the special committee should be struck regardless of the work undertaken by that parliamentary committee. Following the tabling today of the supplementary estimates by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), that caution is even more important than at the time of the tabling of the green paper.
I understand that the powers the committee is to have, as outlined in the motion, are fairly straightforward, and I do not want to deal with them at any length.
Since the tabling of the green paper on February 3 certain questions in the minds of many of us have been accentuated. The first question I want to mention is minor, but I think vital to the success of this exercise. This question relates to the simple fact that the green paper is not available. I hope the minister and the government will take it upon themselves to effect wide distribution of the green paper. If we want public debate we must get this document in the hands of those who are to react and take part in the debate.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: We can't afford that.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In view of the spending estimates, perhaps we cannot afford that. I understand the highlights are available, and that the complete four-volume green paper costs approximately $12. If we want the Canadian public to react, the green paper should be available. I understand that members have asked for a second copy to be placed in their constituency offices where at least people can come and read it, or perhaps take it home for a few days, but even that request has been denied because apparently copies are not available. I want to impress upon the minister that it is vital that this information be placed in the hands of Canadians. I am not trying to be picayune, but I
Immigration Green Paper
think this is a matter that should be looked at with great speed by the minister.
The second matter which has come to my attention since the tabling of the green paper is the impression a number of people have that this is simply a public relations exercise on which we are now embarking in that really the decisions have already been made by the government, and that all the discussion and debate on the green paper are designed to reinforce the tough decisions of the government.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Taking the heat off.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, possibly taking the heat off. I was pleased that the minister in his statement today said he wanted to lay before the Canadian people all the facts, and that he wanted to be frank with the people. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) prides himself on his frankness as well.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: He is frank.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If that is being frank then I had better go back to my dictionary to find out what the definition really is of that word. Let me impress upon the minister and the government that if we want a candid reaction from the Canadian people, and if this exercise is to be meaningful, then we cannot skirt certain issues. I agree that we should not approach this from an Archie Bunker point of view, but rather from a frank point of view as to how the whole population growth and demographic status will effect us as Canadians.
Among the important aspects I think the committee should look into is the type of population growth we really want. I come back to the statement I made on February 3 when the green paper was tabled, that we are looking for an immigration study as a result of which we will hopefully get into a population study. To me that sounds backwards, but that is the approach we are taking.
We must also study what kind of a country we really want, and in this regard certain things have happened since the points system was introduced in 1967 which have had an effect on the make-up of our Canadian population. I hope the committee will be very frank in its analysis and report to the government on this aspect.
Another aspect the committee must consider involves regional differences. It is true that more than 50 per cent of the immigrants who come here go to our three major cities. There are specific conditions which have resulted in this allocation that the committee must consider. At the same time there are regions in Canada to which immigrants have not gone in great numbers, where today they are still welcome because of the requirement to fill the jobs available. The committee must also consider the whole question of migrant labour.
Yesterday I saw a program televised on the national CTV network called "Inquiry". That program bothered me because of its negative approach to an unusual immigration question. If we are to approach these questions from a negative point of view we will run into trouble as a nation. We are not going to get the candidness and frankness we need in order to make the long term decisions necessary.

March 3, 1975
Immigration Green Paper
Another matter the committee must study is third world immigration, or immigration from those countries from which we traditionally have not received many people. Again may I say that I hope the committee can look at this question frankly and fairly, and that once having received as much information as is available it can then come in with a recommendation that will be acceptable to most Canadians.
Further, there is a question which has been skirted by many people since the tabling of the green paper. I refer to the question of francophone immigration. As the government indicated in its statement of October 22, 1974, the new immigration is to be related directly to job availability. If this is so, then we should look critically at the situation to see whether we are to use immigration as a vehicle to promote the ratio which presently exists between English and French speaking Canadians. I am not trying to be divisive in this regard. However, I feel that often this is a question which lurks in the background of people's minds but is not answered. This is a question which should be looked at fairly, critically and objectively.
More division is created merely by saying this is a question which must be looked at, but once it has been looked at we must arrive at a consensus. I think the government should be looking at this in that spirit. It will be necessary to have public reaction in respect of this and other matters which I cannot mention now because of the time available. I want to impress upon the government very strongly that if it wishes to have the views of the Canadian people it should ask for those views, and then accept them. I say to the government that it should not ignore the views of the public as being unimportant.
There is a third matter which I believe should be placed before this House prior to the establishment of the committee. I refer to the time frame in which the committee is to work. From my understanding of the minister's words and from my reading of the motion it appears that the committee is to complete its work in Ottawa, is to travel to various cities in Canada, and then is to write its report by July 31, 1975.
The second part of the schedule is that the minister hopes he can prepare legislation on the basis of the information received, which is to be presented to the House in the fall of 1975, and he hopes that the immigration legislation will be passed early in 1976. I, and many members of this House know that a new immigration act is desperately needed. The last act, which dates back to 1952, has been amended many times. Unfortunately there have been more regulatory amendments than specific legislative amendments passed by this House.
While I concede the minister's schedule, the time frame concerns me somewhat. It is a massive process we are to undertake. Let us be frank about that. If we are to have large scale public input and dissemination of the information received, the undertaking will be massive. The members of this House who will be members of the special committee have other obligations and responsibilities. So the task is a large one.
[Mr. Epp.)
I fear that the stricture of the July 31 date will create a difficult situation. I fear that there may be a number of groups who will not have an opportunity to react, or that the committee or sub-committees will visit the major centres of Canada and that the smaller centres might not have a visit from the committee or sub-committees. Because of this many people may not have an opportunity to react to the green paper or present their views. As a result there may be complaints from many people that they did not have an opportunity to present their views.
I want to place a caveat on the record on behalf of my party. While we recognize the minister desires this schedule in respect of the study of the green paper, the date of July 31 is of great concern to us. While I do not intend to appear pessimistic or negative, I feel that in the initial stages the process will be agonizing because many of the questions strike at the very fundamental approach and attitude Canadians have taken in respect of this country.
We have welcomed groups of various backgrounds to this country where they can make their own way. After the initial reaction has been received when the committee has started travelling, after the views of Canadians have been received, I wonder whether the time frame is sufficient to provide for a period when Canadians will have a chance to think again, and reach a consensus in respect of this democratic Canadian goodwill. I would hope that the time frame would be such as to provide an immigration policy which recognizes all the population and allows a democratic approach to the question. Therefore I wish to impress upon the minister and the government very clearly that while the July 31 date is embodied in the motion it causes me a great deal of concern.
There is another problem which has come to my mind since the tabling of the green paper. I should like a reaction from the minister in this regard. I have received reports from immigration and customs officers who fear that a large number of people will soon enter Canada illegally because of their fear that restrictions will be imposed on immigration. There is a feeling that amnesty will have to be provided again in the not too distant future because it would be difficult to deport the large number of people who might be involved. I should like to impress upon the minister that it is incumbent on the officials of his department to be very wary in this situation.
In conclusion may I say that this party welcomes the work that is before us even though we see it as a massive undertaking. We are willing to co-operate; we are willing to co-operate on the basis of goodwill and frankness, on the basis that this will be discussed freely and that any information which is needed, which is accessible to the government and to no one else, will be made available to the committee and to members of the public in order that the final result will be that the committee will have travelled across Canada, that public hearings will have been held, and that out of this will have flowed an immigration policy that is fair, one with which most Canadians can identify, and that the result will be beneficial to all of us.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the establishment of this committee. I am opposed not only because it is to be a Senate committee
March 3, 1975

but also on the basis that if we are to look at the whole problem of immigration, which I doubt, then we should do it in as straightforward a manner as possible. If the other place is to be the place of sober second thought, then it should not make the original decision.
I suppose that there have been more changes made in the immigration program since 1952 because of the administration of that program than there have been in most programs. In fact the present immigration program bears little relationship to previous programs because of changes in administration. I would go so far as to say that it does not matter what the committee does, whom it hears and how extensive the opposition is, because officials in the minister's department have already made up their mind on the kind of immigration act they want to have, and the criteria on which it should be based.
I presume that if they wanted to, within two weeks the officials could present us with an amended immigration act. Evidence collected by the committee in its travelling across the country will do absolutely nothing to change their minds even though the committee's travels might stir up a lot of opinions that are under the surface and have not come to light.
It is a fact that in the last few years we have taken precautions not to establish a quota system but to change the regulations so as to establish exactly how many people we can allow into the country. We know how to stall in one area so as not to have more medical doctors coming in, and we know how to handle the situation in other areas where there is a need for doctors. We even know how much money it costs us to advertise to keep the right balance in this regard. All that has been done by the administration of the program, not by policy, not in accordance with the wishes of the Canadian public, and also not necessarily against their wishes. It is my personal opinion that this has been a fairly satisfactory arrangement.
I am aware of the fact that many people have been brought into the country, but it is interesting to remember that the last Immigration Act was brought in less than ten years after we actually established Canadian citizenship. Before that we were all British subjects, so the changes that have been made were drastic changes made in a relatively short period of time.
I am one of those who think that the immigration policy is not a complete mistake. This has never been more apparent than when the public was consulted and asked to accept refugees. This happened after the second world war, and since then from time to time when serious problems have developed throughout the world and certain countries were asked to accept immigrants on a refugee status. Most people will agree that in accepting those refugees we did not upset the balance we had already established, that in fact we maintained it by accepting people from various parts of the world, in spite of heavy immigration from central Europe after the war.
I suggest that the committee in travelling around the country and hearing representations in the short period of time given to it will not provide the public with the opportunity to express itself as to whether or not a defi-
Immigration Green Paper
nite and strong control should be exercised over the type of people we bring into Canada, as to the countries from which we bring those people and, much more important, where we should establish them in Canada.
We are well aware of the fact that in this country we have been plagued with pressure groups which have had a great deal of influence on officials in the Department of Manpower and Immigration. For example, let us consider the problem we have had with the medical profession. We have followed an open door policy with regard to medical people from any part of the country on two or three occasions, but recently we changed that position to one of almost total restriction. Medical associations in Toronto have said repeatedly that they have enough doctors in the province-although they turn out doctors from Ontario medical schools in limited numbers only-that they do not want any more doctors brought in because it will cut down on their incomes.
Almost all of the pressure groups have failed to take into consideration the needs of the population, and that involves the basic problem which the minister has mentioned on a number of occasions, namely, the difference between immigration to urban centres and immigration to the rural areas of Canada. It is true that the medical profession does not want any more doctors in Toronto than already there, and it wants only certain types of doctors or specialists, but it could certainly allow a large number of additional doctors to settle in other parts of Ontario, such as communities in parts of northern Ontario, which covers more than half the province, where doctors in every specialty and in every category are desperately needed.
Immigrant doctors are being prevented from practising there because the number of doctors in the province is restricted, and most are to be found in urban centres. Obviously medical associations are in control of the situa-. tion through hospital boards. The same is true with regard to plumbers and other trades and professions. They have methods of bringing about changes in the administration of the act.
I do not see how that situation can change in six months. I do not see how we will be able, in talking to people, to obtain an unbiased opinion as to whether or not it would be wise to decentralize our population growth, whether it would not be wise to bring in immigrants to rural areas in such a way as to have them stay there. I know that this poses many problems. When displaced persons came to Canada after the second world war they came on condition that they stay for two years in the job which they were originally given. Many of them stayed longer.
However, now we are interested in bringing in people for employment in mining, forestry and all types of development in the mid-Canada corridor where most of our resources are located. Where do most immigrants settle? Obviously they gravitate towards large centres of population, because in most cases, that is where their friends are and where they assimilate best. Also, they can find employment there easiest. In other areas of Canada, efforts will have to be made to find them employment.
In my own area in the last few years a number of people of Dutch origin have arrived and settled. At first they had

March 3, 1975
Immigration Green Paper
much difficulty and put a lot of effort into starting in farming operations in a small way. However, in only eight or ten years most of them have become pretty successful. I think that we were ill advised in placing them in that kind of community and asking them to start at the bottom, because if we provided them with some incentive they could become efficient producers right away because they are mainly well trained and they adapt to the community very well. However, they do not have money, and we do not help them make a go of it.
I am sure the minister will say that it is very hard to make people settle in a certain area, and I think that is true. I have often thought that possibly the Arab-Israeli problem could be solved if we brought either the Israelis or the Arabs-or perhaps even both-and put them somewhere in the sub Arctic region where they would have to make a go of it. Both are very enterprising peoples and would make a go of it, but the difficulty would be in keeping them there. That is an extreme position, however, and I am not really advocating it.
However, I do believe that we will have to bring people from other countries and that they must fit in, not in four or five generations but right away, and help develop the area where they settle. That does not appear to me, as a person from Northern Ontario, to be the city of Toronto. It does not need any more people. As one hon. member said, all that would do is establish a nation of Archie Bunkers. That is already happening, of course. If you ride the streetcar in Toronto you can hear people ask why foreigners are allowed into the country to take their jobs.
Of course one could easily stir up prejudice across the country; this government did that once and found there was more prejudice than it could handle. It is important, however, that the government have some indication of where prejudice exists. It is one thing to ask a man who works in a factory in Toronto what his position is on immigration, but it is another to ask someone who has been laid off his job and then sees someone else get it. The answers are likely to be quite different.
I believe the minister and his department have decided what the bill is to contain, and that this preliminary discussion is just an exercise in futility. His officials have studied the problem firsthand year in and year out. It is not something that developed overnight. We are not going to depopulate the over populated parts of the world and see how many people we can fit into Canada. Of course I do not think the minister is suggesting any such thing, nor is he suggesting that we should decide what the population should be by the year 2000 and work toward that target.
Immigration will be accepted in this country as long as it flows in harmony with our needs and ability to absorb it. We have never had a closed door immigration policy, and we should not start now. If the government wants to develop an immigration policy that is acceptable to the people I think it should first tackle the problem of urbanization.
Immigration officials, and persons connected with the other agencies who have close contact with the people who arrive in Canada daily, will be able to inform the commit-

tee of the problems they encounter. They know the difficulties that an immigration policy must tackle for certain classes and types of immigrants. I am not opposed to allowing the department to make the decision on what direction we want that policy to move. They are the people with the expertise, although certainly the minister must put his foot down every now and again to make sure that they retain a touch of humanity. I have not been unhappy about the flow of immigration, but I have been somewhat unhappy about the distribution and the rush to the major cities.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the minister would do better to introduce his new immigration act today rather than wait the six months he has allocated for this exercise. I listen to the hotline programs, as I am sure the minister does, so we know the prejudices that exist in the country-there are probably as many prejudices as there are citizens. Over the years I think Canadians for the most part have welcomed people from all countries and all ethnic backgrounds, and such people have helped build the Canadian mosaic. In most cases, Canadians felt they were sharing with the newcomers the resources that we have in abundance.
It should always be borne in mind that it does not really matter how poorly the immigrant is educated or from which country he comes. When immigrant children grow up and attend Canadian schools they are assimilated, because they are just as intelligent and have as much ability as anybody else. They have just as good a chance of getting ahead and making a contribution to the nation as the other children. When I worked in the mines many of the people there were almost illiterate, but their children grew up to make a name for themselves across the country and become a credit to the community.
We must be careful not to develop prejudice. We must not tell people that they have to speak French or have to speak English, or if they are Italian that they must go to Toronto, or if they are Greek that they must go to a Greek community. The minister's green paper exercise may well encourage resentment and prejudice. I am sure the minister can avoid this. If he heeds the kinds of recommendations normally made by a committee and by special interest groups, I am sure he can amend the Immigration Act and enable it to do the sort of job it has always done.
I put it to the minister that we are not dissatisfied with the results of immigration. Immigrants to Canada have become a credit to this country. Sure, some objected to Chilean refugees entering on the ground they might be Marxists; others objected, after World War II, to displaced persons from Europe entering, on the ground some of them might be Nazis. I am sure that some of these fears were well founded. All the same, one generation after the entry of these immigrants, what do you find? In almost every community the immigrants and their descendants have made a fine contribution to our national fabric. Yes, some of them are in this House. So do not let us say that we need immigrants only from England, or France, or that we need to keep the Chinese balance, or that we need more Italians and Greek people.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Don't forget the Swedes.
March 3, 1975

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We must not forget the Swedes and Norwegians. The Nordic peoples never needed much defending. They always defended themselves. They are not prejudiced, and people are not prejudiced against them. But, Mr. Speaker, we do not want the kind of prejudice I am speaking about stirred up now.
Why does the minister want a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to study this question?
I know that Mr. Dawson called the Senate the place of sober second thoughts, but the minister wants those sober second thoughts at the beginning of the discussion. The members of this House are elected; the members of the Senate are not. I therefore think unless we had a referendum, that if we are to investigate the wishes, aspirations and desires of the Canadian people on immigration, the members of the House of Commons should conduct the investigation. Once we pass a bill the Senate will have the right to amend, or to consider it with sober second thought. Of course, the Senate will do nothing of the kind. It is largely composed of Liberals, and Liberals will dominate the committee. The minister is trying to kill two birds with one stone, and I object.
In any event, Mr. Speaker ruled the other day, in connection with another matter, that co-operation between this House and the other place is not always desirable. I think the standing orders of the other place prohibit it in certain instances. Why ask for the establishment of a joint committee to study immigration?
The minister might be influenced by the fact that the other place is to be covered by CBC television. Probably the minister and other members want to bask in the reflected glory of Senators who may enjoy exposure on national television. I hope that is not what the minister wants.
A new immigration policy will only last for about 20 years; after that, because circumstances change, the policy will change. That being so, the committee in its travels across the country must exercise caution in making sure that it does not bring forward prejudices rather than ideas. As the woman appearing on television the other night in Toronto said, after the green paper has been given a full airing we may become a nation of Archie Bunkers, with every person looking over his shoulder at his neighbour. This has not happened before in this country, and I hope it never will. Canadians are charitable; they know their country is rich and are willing to share its riches.
Canadian immigration policies have worked to the advantage of Canada. Ethnic groups who have entered this country have made their contribution to Canada. Most become Canadians. The second generation, the descendants of immigrants, are pretty nearly indistinguishable from those who welcomed the original immigrants.
The minister's officials no doubt have ready a draft of the legislation which is to be presented some time after July. No doubt it could be introduced in this House within the next two weeks. In any event I suggest that the minister should seek his consensus from the Canadian population without raising the spectre of prejudice. Quite possibly the minister's suggested way of proceeding will not result in harmony being established. Possibly, the information he seeks can be obtained only by a full investigation. In any event I strongly urge the minister to
Immigration Green Paper
appoint a committee of this House only. Let us not make it a joint committee, a committee on which the other place will be represented. A joint committee should not consider the proposed legislation before it is even presented to this House.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO REFER GREEN PAPER TO SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the motion of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) for the appointment of a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to collect the views across the country of the citizens concerned about immigration, with a view to reorienting or reviewing the Canadian immigration policy.
Mr. Speaker, this debate need not be lengthy to be useful, this afternoon, since in the final analysis we are asked to decide whether or not a committee will be appointed, and if so, what its powers will be.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk of immigration, when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration launches a debate by publishing a green paper and distributing it across the country-I have here the briefs submitted by our fellow citizens on this important subject-he must expect that the debate will not be limited strictly to immigration as such. Canada is not a closed country, nor can it be. We cannot erect a fence around Canada and say: In the future, no immigrant may enter Canada. Obviously not. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, when immigrants are being recruited for Canada in their native lands, this recruitment must obviously be done in terms of the objectives and interests of Canada.
An immigration policy cannot be formulated that will please all the countries in the world to the detriment of Canada. That immigration policy must respect the objectives and interests of all Canadians from sea to sea. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is what was wrong with our immigration policy in the past. In many cases, immigrants have been required to do what is commonly known as the dirty work, seasonal jobs, as is now the case, for instance, in Quebec in a certain conflict at Louiseville, of which the minister has been informed. Workers are brought in to do a certain job and are then left to fend for themselves in the administrative mess of immigration. This shows, Mr. Speaker, that there is a problem in Canadian manpower as far as certain jobs are concerned, and that the present Immigration Act is often made flexible in the interest of the government but not of the immigrants.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, how are immigrants recruited? How are they selected? What kind of an investigation is made about these immigrants? When they arrive in Canada, how are they received, regardless if their native country? It is important that Canada, since we want and need immigrants, receive them sensibly and in an orderly fashion. Let us imagine a foreigner who arrives in Canada to stay and asks for immigrant status and who is left on his own, very often with language difficulties. What becomes of him? He will depend on the government to survive instead of being able to find for himself.
There are some great Canadians of foreign origin, and we all feel that the majority of immigrants have made a

March 3, 1975
Immigration Green Paper
very important contribution to Canada. We have only to think about the construction of the railroad in the West to realize that without the immigrants, this railroad could never have been built when it was by Mr. Macdonald. This is only one example among hundreds that show the important contribution of these people.
Mr. Speaker, I know personally several immigrants from my constituency in Montreal and in Quebec City. Many of them were faced with enormous difficulties from immigration offices when they tried to obtian their residence permits and Canadian citizenship. They did not receive from government agencies quite the reception they needed to integrate fully into Canadian society. You will hear these immigrants complain that Canadians point the finger of scorn at their children, for Canada is not yet mature enough to accept immigrants who have skins of a different colour and who speak a foreigh language.
Mr. Speaker, there is a humanitarian aspect to immigration which must not be overlooked.
Based on these general considerations, I feel that this committee will have many parts to play and will have an important function, depending on the orientation the minister chooses to give it. First of all, it will have to listen to what Canadians have to say about immigration and immigrants into this country. Then it will have to listen to what immigrants have to say about the current policy which many of them had to stand. Third, we will have to promote an effective dialogue and not merely a monologue between the Canadian people and the immigrants, so that we may establish together an immigration policy serving the interests of both the Canadian people, especially the economic and social interests of manpower, and the immigrants.
Mr. Speaker, such were the few comments I wanted to make in that connection. In conclusion, I would like to point out that Quebec is experiencing a serious decline in its birth rate. Moreover, statistics show without doubt that immigration has not always serve the Quebec interests. God knows that I am not a separatist and I would like to repeat it to the minister, I believe in Canada. I feel that immigration can help Quebec. Mr. Speaker, when establishing a national policy on immigration the distinctive entity of each Canadian province will have to be maintained.
By then, the minister will certainly have taken a step forward. The present Immigration Act is discriminatory in respect to the distribution of immigrants because of the advertising about the provinces of Quebec, Ontario or British Columbia, so that, in the last analysis, this policy has been detrimental to the general interests of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, in many instances, immigrants are not advised that the language spoken in Quebec is French. On his arrival in Canada, the immigrant feels lost in cities like Quebec, Victoriaville, Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivieres or Chicoutimi, because he does not know the language spoken there. He had not been told about it.
I believe the committee will have to consider this matter. Basic data will have to be provided so that the citizens of every province, and particularly the people in

Quebec, may be consulted so that an immigration policy useful to every province may be developed.
I can see the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party (Mr. Stanfield) in the House. He once was a provincial Premier and he should be in a position to back what I say. It is important for provincial governments that our immigration policy should be one of help, and should not lead to frustrations, problems or troubles, especially in a province where in some respects the problem for immigrants is of a linguistic nature.
Mr. Speaker, I must add that, unfortunately, a great many Canadians resent the coming of immigrants to Canada. I am not one of them. However, I have to admit that Canadians are right in their often harsh but also positive criticism of immigration. How many Canadian families, they say, are unemployed, how many workers in Canada, in Victoriaville or elsewhere are unemployed, have difficulties with their governments, are the object of disrespect in their relationships with civil servants and public agencies? How many Canadians feel frustrated because of the economical, political or social situation? Mr. Speaker, we shall re-open the door to immigration some way or other to bring in labour in Canada.
According to Chapter 14, page 17 of the Green Paper, with respect to funds alloted to immigration, $41,718,000 are spent for immigration purposes in general. Mr. Speaker, that is a considerable amount of money to bring in manpower, and every time we do so we bring in new problems. Maybe our manpower policy is a negative one. Our present labour policy deters Canadian workers from working in particular areas. It is definitely outdated, definitely not adapted to our automation, modernistic society, and I think neither the Minister nor the Committee should restrict themselves to the only matter of immigration. They will have to agree to broaden the scope of this public debate for the impact of the immigration year on Canadian labour to be studied.
Mr. Speaker, should we heartily welcome in Canada 10,000 perfect immigrants in all respects, serious people, industrious, honest people, if at the same time Canadian workers were denied certain jobs and those immigrants were given preference, I think, Mr. Speaker, that in such a case the immigration policy would not serve the immigrants' interests since they would be put into conflict with Canadians. Neither would the immigration policy serve the Canadians' interests since they would be put into conflict with the immigrants and would be deprived of an eventual job. Finally, this immigration policy would have been a source of frustration and division in our country rather than unification of Canadians.
We will build our country, because immigration policy will contribute to the building of a country, to the extent where before speaking of immigration we will be willing to make good use of our labour, in order that Canadians can work according to their characteristics, their tastes, their personality, their creativity, before providing immigrants with similar jobs or calling in Canada other people.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, on that extremely important issue of the scandal that took place in Louisville-I call that a scandal, it is disgusting-I say those things should not happen in 1975.
March 3, 1975

In Louiseville, a certain company brought in manpower to do a kind of work, and at the end when they ran out of work, before the department and other people saw to it, and especially before those people got going, they wanted to send the immigrants back home. It is a bit like what happened in the case of the Haitians.
Mr. Speaker, I find it scandalous to displace foreigners who are our brothers, humans of other countries, to bring them here, and then get rid of them and send them back. If Canadians do not want to do certain jobs, it proves that our manpower policies-not necessarily Canadians-are wrong. Even if UIC officials, public investigators who run around, instead of looking for cheaters, to catch Canadians, strangle them and make them pay fines because they allegedly cheated the government, I say that efforts should be made to encourage Canadians to work. Then, Mr. Speaker, Canadians would believe a lot more in the future of their country. When that becomes a reality it is sure that with their pride and their nationalism they will be happy to share their national pride with people from other countries. Let us not ask Canadians to accept immigrants, whatever their origin, their language, their race or their religion, without knowing first if Canadians are ill-treated or forgotten. Mr. Speaker, if we want Canadians to really participate in the life of this country, if we want an immigration policy to really be valid and effective Canadians themselves must not apply it at home.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is a bad habit in this House when a special joint committee is set up and travels across the country to examine a question, there is a bad habit of sending such committees to larger centres-Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec City sometimes. Indeed, I am quite convinced there are as many people in Victoriaville in my area, in Trois-Rivieres, Drummondville or Saint-Hyacinthe who have as many valuable views as people in Montreal or Toronto. I think that people in Toronto and Montreal did not invent anything. They do not have the monopoly of truth, Mr. Speaker.
If the minister is serious and really logical, if he wishes to raise a public debate at the national level, I think he should manage to convince the members of this committee to hold more than one hearing in the Northwest Territories, in Yukon, in Whitehorse, Saint John, Quebec City, Montreal, Toronto or Ottawa and not say goodbye, our terms of reference were for six months only.
Mr. Speaker, if the minister really wants Canadians to participate and really wants to know their views, I think we should go also in small urban centres and even in rural communities. How many immigrants went to settle in these areas or in small towns like Victoriaville or Drummondville? How many? It could be surprising, but they are many. This is why there are Canadians in Victoriaville, Drummondville, Saint-Hyaeinthe, Trois-Rivieres, who have to welcome immigrants. Those Canadians should be given the opportunity to express their views concerning the formulation of such a policy.
Lastly Mr. Speaker, there is an example I wish to mention. I had a friend from France who was told that he could come to Canada with the teaching degrees he had. He left his position in France and came to Canada in a municipality that I shall not name as it is small and everyone would know who it is.
Grain
Then he came to Canada and the Quebec government never recognized his degrees. He had to go back to France at his own expenses. He had to make a general collect, to beg and return directly to France. Mr. Speaker, he had become my friend and could have made a good Canadian but because he had been misinformed he returned to France with a poor opinion about our country. I feel sorry about it because he could have made an excellent Canadian and because he returned there and will reflect a bad image of Canada. But he talks about what he saw, what he felt, and he has had a bad experience.
Mr. Speaker, I think that if the Minister wants to start a profitable dialogue with the population, he must expect that the discussion will not be restricted to the question of immigration. The whole question of immigration will have to be debated, that is from the leave from the country of origin to the moment of arrival in the host country, and the manpower policy will have to be taken into account. I think the minister must expect, anyway, that the Social Credit party will make representations on the judicious use of Canadian manpower to encourage our families, our workers; then we can speak positively about immigration. Only under those conditions, Mr. Speaker, will an immigration policy serve both the interests of immigrants and those of Canada.
Motion agreed to.
