subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I at long last rise to introduce this motion. Having been a member of the House for a few years I have repeatedly placed a motion such as this on the order paper, and hoped that at some time we might give consideration to this problem. I have been concerned about this matter for a good many years, as have many other members of the House, and as I am sure have others outside the House.
When one lives in a rural community one comes to realize that there are many in our society who are underprivileged, and one has the opportunity to meet poverty face to face. Many of us have known people who have struggled in their endeavours to provide a livelihood for themselves in one form or another. Some have 'met with tremendous success. Others in our society have, unfortunately, never tasted success.
There are too many people in this category. Many people in our society point the finger at the advances that have been made in social welfare legislation-and there have been many-but I have become concerned at the direction in which some welfare measures have taken us. It seems to me that our system of priorities has somehow become all mixed up, and perhaps it is because of the attempt by the ruling government of the day to cover as many people as possible and to pass many pieces of legislation that protect us, as the saying goes, from the cradle to the grave.
In recent years an attempt has been made to look after a group of people who, to my way of thinking, have not yet equally earned a right to their share of the wealth in this country as have others. In many cases we find the administration of social assistance schemes in the hands of provincial governments. Each provincial government has its own method of administering a program; some have a different set of priorities from others. Generally speaking they all work toward improving the lot of the individual, but some provide more assistance, or more opportunity for assitance.
Thus we have what appears to be a hodge-podge of plans that do not get to what I consider to be the root of a problem affecting too many people in their later years. Many of the people I am concerned with in this particular motion were, if they were fortunate, employed during the depression years, and if one goes back to those years one will remember that not too many industries had pension plans of any kind. Government pension plans in those days were simply ideas that were just taking root; the public treasury could not sustain an elaborate plan, and so many people today do not receive a pension of any sort when they retire. These people who find themselves in the twilight of their years are unable to retire from their fields of endeavour, but must continue in employment when perhaps their health is not such that would justify society
Old. Age Pension
asking them to continue. Thank God there are many who are in good health and are able to continue working.
I do not wish to place upon society a scheme which would be bureaucratically top heavy. Sometimes I believe the most simple way is the best way. We should be introducing programs through a system of evolution in such a way that we do not penalize those in our society who are paying the taxes, but at the same time look after the needs of others. We should have a system which allows those who are not able to continue actively in employment to retire. These people have surely earned this right.
Many of the schemes which have been in effect are meagre, and here I think of some of the pension plans the railway companies have had over the years. While there has been some form of pension scheme, many will argue that the pensions received in no way take into account the tremendous inflationary pressures we face today. It is time for the government to take into account those who have been employed in industry and who receive meagre pensions. It is also time for the government to take into account the self-employed people who have not contributed, in any way over the years, toward plans.
I think also of the many thousands of Indian people who have lived a very hard life yet have never had the opportunity to earn an appreciable income. There are many people today who are accustomed to working and are still struggling while this society seems bent upon relieving the pressure on other groups, and I think here of the young people. Some of the plans we have come up with may be admirable, and they may meet some need, but too often we hear the complaint that too many young people are on welfare while too many old people are unable to receive assistance.
I wonder why it is that we think it proper to move in areas such as unemployment insurance to relieve the stresses that may be inherent in not being able to earn a living, while at the same time we do not take into account the needs of those people, 60 years and over, who are unable to receive any form of assistance, and here I think of those who have applied for assistance which has been denied because of the invariable regulations that require them to dispose of all the possessions they have in order to qualify.
I have not framed my motion in such a way that we would suddenly be burdened with a huge tax bill in order to accomplish the goals set forth. I have suggested to the government that consideration be given to granting immediate pensions to women 60 years of age and over. In many instances such women have never been employed in industry. It is only in recent years that more and more women have been going into the labour market.
In many cases the men who have been the breadwinners have been employed in industry the nature of which has shortened their life expectancy. I think of those employed in the lumber industry, for example. No longer can those people be expected to go out into the bush and suffer the elements, as they have in the past, in order to continue to provide for themselves and their families. I think also of some of the evidence regarding employment in the mining industry. Very recently we were disturbed about what was
3728

Old Age Pension
taking place in the asbestos mines. These people must continue to work, but they know that by doing so they are shortening their lives. Many of them would like to retire, yet they must continue because under our system a pension is not available until age 65. Our society must take a serious look at situations of this kind.
It is perfectly all right for the government to suggest it is moving in the direction of a guaranteed income plan, but the simple fact is that it will be many years before this is an accomplished fact. Such a scheme involves provincial participation. While there may be a willingness on the part of some provinces to participate in this scheme, the government will have to overcome many obstacles.
There are many people in our society who believe there is something proper about working for a living, and I belong to that group. There are a good many people who feel we have gone too far already with our welfare schemes. I am sure there will be resistance to the government moving in the direction of a guaranteed income plan. There are so many unknown factors involved in the 10 provinces participating in such a plan that it would be unwise for the government to move in that direction in haste. The government has been working on plans to be used as a test in certain areas, but before we get all the answers to our questions time will have moved on; it is this precious time that is of the essence, particularly when one considers that every day that goes by one is closer to the end.
There are many people of age 60 who are no longer capable of carrying on in their traditional employment. I have some statistics which indicate that the average age of a farmer today is 57. I personally know of many who would be prepared to sell off whatever small possessions they might have in order to retire, but because of the uncertainty of the agricultural economy they are obliged to continue working.
I am afraid we may be too late if we should move in the direction indicated by the government, which is the direction of an annual income for everyone. In that case many people may not receive any benefit. I am sure every member of this House is familiar with such cases in many parts of this country. A lot of these people have laid the foundation of our society as we know it today. They have done a good job.
The least amount of criticism one hears about the various plans we have in different welfare categories relates to the area of old age security. I am always dubious concerning plans which involve means tests in order that people may qualify. Many people find it very humiliating to have to announce to the world that, after a period of 60 years, they have failed. So they quietly shrug their shoulders and bury themselves in their little homes or apartments, living on what they have. I do not think this should be necessary.
One remembers the type of criticism we heard in respect of the old age pension being universal. We were given examples of millionaires, and there were a few around us in this House. The suggestion was made that millionaires would receive the benefit. I do not believe that is either a correct or fair approach. At income tax time one could give

a few examples. We must realize that a transfer of payment is involved and that it goes back to the government. One might look at the number of public servants who will be required this coming year. One realizes that it is not in our general interest to build up a bureaucracy, because not only is it a federal bureaucracy that would have to be built up to administer any plan which would take into account any guaranteed income which may be perceived, but there is also the provincial bureaucracy that will be involved. Perhaps this is something we lose sight of, Mr. Speaker.
We must realize that it is not only the salaries of these employees which would be involved but also the cost of offices and general administration. In a sense there are hidden costs. The easiest way is to have a universal payment for those who have reached the age suggested in my motion.
Now I wish to mention another aspect of this matter. Many people will suggest this is a very costly plan.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: How much will it cost?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
It will cost something in the area of $600 million a year. If one takes into account the total budgetary estimates of public funds, this represents something like two per cent. We must remember that there are something in the order of 817,000 unemployed persons and that many of these people would not receive assistance from the unemployment insurance plan. We must also realize that because of the assistance plans in many provinces it is difficult to estimate the total cost because one cannot calculate the amount that will come back in the form of income tax payments.
In the initial stages my plan would take into account some 380,000 females. There is a progression so far as males are concerned. Some 750,000 individuals would eventually be encompassed. We might look at the entire budgeted estimates for this year.

speechtext:
I thank the House. I shall be very brief.
I certainly do not wish to talk out my own motion. When one thinks of the fact that just over ten years ago our total budget was in the order of approximately $6 billion and now is something in the order of $28 billion, certainly the amount required in this case would be within our means. I ask the House not to talk out this bill but rather to give it careful consideration. In the absence of anything in the way of a guaranteed annual income I ask for this consideration in respect of the people in this particular group.
March 3, 1975

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am grateful that this issue has been brought up by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski). But I find it is the absolute antithesis of equality. While women for too long have been dominated and controlled by men and by society, and while they have been restricted and without independence even in respect of the right to claim a mortgage, I still feel that a bill of this type would be an expression of national guilt, this would be as discriminatory as the past has been to women.
I favour the right of all people, male or female, to retire on pension at age 60 if this can be handled actuarially. But I also believe people should have the right to continue to work as long as they can be productive, since the period between age 60 and 65 is a period of perhaps highest opportunity and highest income in preparation for the inescapable time when we must all live on a fixed income.
Many men and women who have worked since their teens, for virtually 40 years of their lives, and who have contributed to the building of this country may be tired of existing in the work market and should be allowed to retire on pension. I would hope the Canada Pension Plan will one day be such that it can support such early retirement, so that people who have leisure may be able to travel as the young have been able to do in recent years. I want them to be able to travel and perhaps receive subsidies similar to those the young people have been receiving through various grants, while they are still vigorous and young enough to enjoy it.
However, I object to anything which gives special privileges because one is a woman, because one is an Indian, or because one is a Jew. It is inverse discrimination which is abhorrent to me. I think everyone, whether women or otherwise, should receive benefits on the basis of merit and equality.
I object very strenuously to this because it would give the employer the right to allow women to drift back into the position of being compulsorily retired at age 60. Again I say it is essential that we all have the right of choice to retire at a time when we know we can manage on the fixed income that is inevitable during retirement years.
I object to the motion because it is inverse discrimination which is tacit in this recommendation. It is a matter of concern to me that there are people who lean over backward to prove that they are not discriminating. To me this is the danger of such a well intentioned motion. I think it overcompensates for past omissions and discriminations. Perhaps it is a reflection of the national and industrial guilt that men now feel and are expressing.
I must say, however, that women have come a long, long way in the last five years, but unfortunately there are still men who are unaware of women's rightful place in society. When I sit in committees I always see groups of men in top executive positions, and I wait hopefully for the day when women will have the opportunity to become executives themselves with the attendant pensions that go with those higher offices.
I am opposed to any type of discrimination, no matter how well intentioned. I know I am repeating myself, but I learned as a school girl learning grammar that repetition
Old Age Pension
is great for emphasis. So let me tell every one here who might forget it that inverse discrimination is as destructive to society as is discrimination itself.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Over the years there has been too much waste of valuable talent, expertise and experience because of the enforced retirement of people. I do not think retirement should be established according to the calendar-it should be established according to competence. It is vital to Canadians and to Canada that all of us work, and give as long as we are capable of doing so and if we choose to do so.
Perhaps a formula should be worked out between management and employees so that people can work as long as they contribute. Unfortunately, it is always the management's choice when an employee should retire. They can keep people in their employment if they choose to do so, but the employee has no choice. Perhaps some day we will learn not to guide our actions in society by age or by sex but by the worth of the human being.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), I have one or two criticisms to make of the way in which the motion of my friend, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), is worded. But I do not think that that criticism should take us away from the main point of the motion, which is that in one way or another pensions should be made available at the age of 60. In that respect I commend my hon. friend for having put forward a motion that produces a discussion of pensions, and I congratulate him on being lucky enough in the draw to get his motion before the House at this stage of the session. I hope that my motion, which is No. 39, will be reached before the end of the session, and I suspect, by the way the session is going, it will be, Mr. Speaker.
The criticism that has been made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway really is quite valid. Women seek not special privilege; women seek equality. I can understand the feeling of women with respect to a motion that asks for something for them that is not to be made available to women and men alike. That is why I hope that one of these days my motion in this area will be reached, because it calls for pensions under both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to be available to all persons at the age of 60 who are out of the labour market or are prepared to leave it.
I have made this reference to my motion because I think it answers both my friend, the hon. member for Mackenzie, and my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. It answers the hon. member for Mackenzie in that it does not discriminate between men and women; it wants the same benefit made available to both. I suggest that my motion answers an argument put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who seems to be afraid of pensions at a certain age carrying the implication that retirement is being forced. No one is seeking forced retirement. What we are seeking is the possibility of retirement, and there is no possibility of retirement unless adequate pensions are available.
28996-3P/2

March 3, 1975
Old Age Pension
I suggest to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, and to the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell), if she enters this debate a little later, that it is not really heresy to be talking in this place about pensions at an age under 65. Right now it is possible for those who are in the RCMP or in the Canadian armed forces to retire at a younger age. Some of them who have done so would want me to remind the House of the fact that their pensions are not escalated by the cost of living until they reach 60, which is an injustice that ought to be corrected. At any rate, retirement at the age of 48, 50 or 52 is possible for certain persons, namely, those whom I have just mentioned.
It is also a fact that public servants generally are free to retire at the age of 60. They can go on working until they are 65, but they may retire at the age of 60, although their pensions could be less than they would be at 65, depending on how many years of service they have had, and also depending on the level of earnings during their best six years.
In addition to the fact that to all public servants the possibility of retiring at the age of 60 is open, it is possible for some public servants to retire at the age of 55. I refer in particular to those who have 30 years of service. A public servant who is 55 years of age or over and has 30 years in the public service, may retire at that point without any penalty factor in his pension. Thus, at 55 years of age a public servant who has 30 years of service gets 30 times 2 or 60 per cent of the average of his best six years as his pension.
There are instances in the public service today, particularly at higher levels, of persons retiring at ages between 55 and 60 because a reasonable pension is available to them. They are not forced to retire. No pensionable age, in terms of public pensions, forces retirement; it simply makes retirement possible.
I feel very strongly that the time has come when we should seriously amend our legislation to make retirement possible at the age of 60. That is what I seek in my motion. If my hon. friend's motion is talked out, I hope the same will not happen to mine. What I seek in my motion No. 39 is that under both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan persons who are out of the labour market or leave it could get their full pensions at that point.
I want to come back again to the point that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway made about drawing the line between men and women. I am sure that the hon. member for Mackenzie did not mean to do that. He is well intentioned, as the hon. member from across the way said. He wants to get the pensionable age down. I think it is somewhat unfair to lower it to 60 right away for women but to tell men that they have to wait five years in which it would be brought down a year at a time.
The other point I want to make is this, Mr. Speaker. I am very much aware, from my contacts and correspondence, of the great number of women, particularly spinsters and widows, in that age bracket who feel the need of a pension without having to wait until age 65. But I am also conscious of the great number of men, particularly those in

heavy industry who have endured the rat race about as long as they can stand it, who should also be considered for early retirement. Every time we go through an election campaign and I meet thousands of shop workers in my constituency, morning after morning as I greet them the men ask when the pensionable age is going to come down to 60. I often look at a man and think he looks older than I do only to find out he is about 58 and has been working in a foundry or a railway shop or the packing industry or in the needle trades and has been in the rat race for years. It is just as hard for him to keep going to age 65 as it is for a woman.
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway who says "Let's put this on an equal basis"; but I submit that is no reason for taking the other line that she did, that there is something wrong about discussing 60 as a reasonable retirement age. I think that has to come. I remember how we went all through these arguments when I first came to this House. The pension was then payable at age 70 and when we argued for it at age 65 we heard the same arguments that were used today-"We need to work", "You take away the meaning of life" and "The state cannot afford it". But we brought the pensionable age down from 70 to 65, even if we had to do it a year at a time.
I think the pension should be available for all persons, Mr. Speaker, and I think the best criterion to establish is that those persons should be out of the labour market. That would cover spouses between age 60 and 65, male or female, bachelors, spinsters, widows and widowers, but on the one condition-that they are out of the labour market. This leads me to say again that what I find wrong with the government proposal that is to come forward some time this year is that it would provide pensions to spouses between age 60 and 65 where the other spouse, male or female, is 65 or over and is receiving a pension. One thing wrong with that is the means test, but the fundamental thing that is wrong is that it says to some women "You will qualify because you have a husband; you are a spouse in that age bracket", but to other women, spinsters or widows, the pension will not be available. The same can apply to men. A man between age 60 and 65 with a wife over 65 will qualify for a pension. A man who is a widower or a bachelor in the same age bracket will not qualify.
There is just as much wrong with the government's proposal as there is with my hon. friend's proposal, Mr. Speaker. I think the slight difference is that my hon. friend is willing to listen to reason and change his, but it is difficult to change the government once it has laid down its position.
I welcome the motion before us this afternoon. The more times this subject comes up, the better. I enjoyed being here during the years when we got the pensionable age down from 70 to 65 and got the pension increased. The time to get it reduced from age 65 to 60 for all those people no longer in the labour market, is now, right now, today.

Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 37(1) I take this opportunity with the greatest respect to correct the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He seems to have misunderstood or misquoted
March 3, 1975

me. I did not say that I do not favour retirement at age 60. I favour it deeply and feel it is most important. What I said was that I do not want the possibility of it becoming mandatory as it gradually might. I stress strongly that at age 60, people are vigorous and well enough to enjoy travel and they should have the choice. But I did not want it exclusively for women; I want it for all people who chose that course.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suggest that is a correction of what the hon. member said and not a correction of my remarks.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the motion introduced by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski). On reading this motion, I wondered what was really the point of it. The hon. member probably wanted to please women, but I realized, after what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) retorted to him, that he had defeated his object, because the member for Vancouver-Kings-way actually found in that motion a hidden discrimination against women. All the same, I am sure the hon. member who moved that motion was well-intentioned and wanted to give housewives the opportunity to get their pensions at sixty, even though they would have been ahead of the men for once.
Mr. Speaker, the matter of lowering the pension age to 60 is nothing new. We were the first to advocate here the granting of old age security pension. Pensionable age was first set at 70, and then lowered to 65. During two election campaigns we asked that pensionable age be lowered to 60. Ninety percent of the people favoured that move, although the government has been reluctant to do so until now.
We even forced them, during the last election campaign, to promise pensions at 60. Let me say at this point, to set the record straight, that we proposed pensions be paid at 60 only to those who wished to retire, and not as a compulsory move. During the last election, we heard Liberals promising pensions for 60 years old. We thought that we were finally going to get it. We thought this would be available to all Canadians. It has always been my position in this House that when reforms or amendements are proposed to social legislation, the first feature of the legislation should be universality. As soon as one enters into details, into sections of the act, discrimination starts. If pensions were paid at age 60, it would have to be real pension, not the current "gimmick" under which 60 percent comes from old age security and 40 percent from charity groups. One thing should be avoided, namely that the act require hundreds and thousands of inspectors to investigate pensioners' homes to see if they did not hide $100 or $200. This is simply ridiculous, is deriding the aged.
If a pension is paid, it is a pension, period. There should be no other test than birth date. No two bit inspector or civil servant should get into old people's homes to unsettle them and often make them sick. We asked the government a number of times to lower pensionable age to 60 for everybody, men and women, who would like to have it and we added that it should be given to the wife who is under 60, at least 65 today, when she had been staying home without salary. We then thought about the family salary;
Old Age Pension
since the mother stays home, looks after her children, the father's salary is necessarily considered as a family salary; to supplement this salary we asked that the mother be given the same pension as her hunband when the latter reaches pension age. I think it is only fair. It is not discriminatory at all; it is only fair to the mother, in the absence of a better system; we should have the family salary today, the salary of the mother. There is no such salary and there will not be one immediately, at least not with this government.
To prevent discrimination, particularly in Quebec, where when the hunband reaches 65, the couple has to live four or five years only on the hunband's pension, when the mother is three, four or five years younger. That is what I call discrimination. I regard such laws as antisocial. This is why we were asking in these particular cases that the mother be given a pension similar to that of her husband.
Now the government at least says that next fall a pension will be given to the mother of a family at age sixty, but that in principle such pension becomes available at sixty five. But the mother of a family, probably in the fall-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
For the spouse, of course. A pension will be given to the spouse at sixty. I agree. But under what conditions? We say; Well, the spouse should not receive an income. He must have only his pension. Good care should be taken to have it that way. There will again be inquiries upon inquiries so that only 10 per cent of mothers will be able to have a pension. These are all little annoyances, little implications which explain why legislation passed here is effective to the extent of 10 or 12 per cent only.
Mr. Speaker, if this legislation is passed let it be passed for all mothers. The person getting an income pays tax at the end of the year. But that will prevent us from having the pension amount eroded by the small inspectors who are on the look-out thoughout Canada for all those women.
It would be so simple to simplify the legislation. But we complicate everything in the law. During my 15 years in this House, I noticed that laws are always made for technocrats, for higher officials. Let us double, triple the number of high-ranking officials, and everything will go smoothly! The pension, finally, is but a pretext to fill offices with high-ranking officials.
It is about time, when we vote a credit, to think that it should go to the one who needs it and that we should not have to spend two thirds of the amount for inspections and regulations which often nullify the laws we vote here so as to give the least possible. This is how things are being done in this House, we vote, it looks good. Whenever a law is passed, people know about it and say: How marvelous. But in the end, there is nothing left. Why? Because we have a government of officials. It exists for officials and not for the needs of the Canadian people.
I congratulate the hon. member who proposed this motion. I should like it to be more universal and I hope with all my heart that this fall, at least, we do not fail. As to the wives younger than their husband, those from 60 to 65 years, all those who want it, and I am not referring here

March 3, 1975
Old Age Pension
to working wives, as the one I was speaking of a while ago, I can understand her point, I hope the government decides once and for all to give them what they need, what they are entitled to.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) strikes me as being manifestly in contradiction to our whole policy as well as the principles of social justice. When governments develop social security policies, and this applies to this government, and are in the process of planning social security changes, the most important consideration they must bear in mind is the equity of the measures they propose to introduce. The hon. member alluded to this government's system of priorities. I think he said something about their being all mixed up. I shall return to that point.
As I said, governments must consider the equity of their measures. By that, I mean they must avoid discrimination in setting varying eligibility conditions and benefits based on artificial distinctions, such as sex, which may be unrelated, or occupation, which may be totally irrelevant. To my mind, the hon. member's proposal for lowering the general pensionable age to 60 is not serious. Personally, I think there is much to be said for lowering the pensionable age to 60; but the economics, the cost, as mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) last year, is astronomical. I think the minister said that this proposal would cost $1.2 billion per year.
Governments must strive to treat all people equally. Their attempt to do this was demonstrated by the recently entered into federal-provincial agreement for removing from the Canada Pension Plan differences in benefits based on sex. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has spoken about differences in CPP benefits based on sex. As I say, these differences have now been eliminated. The position of the government of Canada is this; Different retirement ages for men and women would constitute discrimination. This discrimination has been eliminated.
If we agree that the principle of a good social security review is valid, we should be wrong in endorsing the sort of motion we are discussing today. The government is committed to removing discriminatory provisions from existing federal legislation and, to this end, has introduced the omnibus bill on the status of women as well as amendments to superannuation legislation and legislation affecting other federal pensions. No one denies the tenuous position of many housewives whom the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin) rightly defined as house mistresses. I truly believe that the problem such women face has moved out of the realm of pure biology and into the realm of economics. I wish to consider it from that angle.
Early retirement for women, as for men, may actually be discriminatory. But let us consider for a moment the implications of early retirement within our present inflationary context, a context in which nearly all feel compelled to re-assess lifestyles because of the rapidly deteriorating purchasing power of incomes. A Financial Times survey carried out not long ago, and based on a study by 28

leading Canadian and United States companies, indicated that the great North American dream of early retirement is in trouble, apparently because of inflation and poor planning. In brief, most of these consultants, according to the same study, seem to agree that the best advice to give these people at this time is to keep working.
There is yet another important factor which governments must not overlook, quite apart from the costs such a scheme would incur. I am referring to the question of priorities. There is no doubt, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare himself pointed out, if the state were a limitless reservoir of funds, it would certainly lower the eligibility age to 60. It so happens the government is not an inexhaustible source of funds. Hence, priorities must be established and respected. That in fact, is the responsibility, the burden of governments and indeed a responsibility which lies not only with the federal government but with the provincial governments as well.
Choices must be made and decisions must take into account the total existing requirements. True, our policies must meet the needs of our older citizens and even, if need be, before retirement. However, along with these, we must also cope with the problems facing the disabled and the handicapped. We must supplement the income of the working-poor. We must implement programs to encourage the low-wage earners to remain in the labour forces. For those who can work, but are without a job, we must find ways and means to allow them to do so. Moreover, there is the single mother whose income is either non-existent or unacceptably low. We must remember housing needs, social services, such as day-care centres, and so on. From these various needs a rational list of priorities must be drawn by order of importance.
The question of income naturally leads us to yet another facet of equity in a social security context, income distribution. In this respect, just how equitable would the adoption of a motion such as the one being discussed today be in terms of allowing all income groups in our society to recoup a fair share of the nation's revenue. I find it difficult to see the motion in this context.
Although one could hardly claim to have exhausted the many aspects of the problem, I trust hon. members of the House by now have dismissed the proposed motion as irrational and unwise. By adopting this measure, the government would only commit a recurring mistake, one for which several other governments could be reproached, that is the single-minded pursuit of one overriding policy objective at the expense of all others. That is completely unacceptable at this time. It is the government's duty to demonstrate wisdom in discerning between first and secondary priorities, and quite often the only choice open to us is to compromise between these priorities.
As a last thought, Mr. Speaker, I might add that my Liberal colleagues and I are far from being insensitive to the problems of the elderly. The record of the Liberal government attests to that. I strongly believe we have to weigh the problems pertaining to senior citizens in relation to all the other problems, and the ability of this country to pay for the solution of them.
March 3, 1975

The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) stated that he felt this proposal could justifiably be included in this $28 billion budget. I do not know what part of the budget he would eliminate in order to accommodate this proposal. I do not believe, in view of the sum total of the budget, this measure is justified, at this time, although in years to come possibly it could be if we reduced the pensionable age to 60. This or subsequent governments would not reduce the pensionable age to 60 on a voluntary basis without any compromises.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare stated in this House that the solution to our problems in social security lies, not through bringing about a broad expansion, or a general lowering of pension benefits to those who are 60 or 55, but rather through a system of guaranteed income or income supplementation, which would be available to all, regardless of age, former occupation, present condition, or sex. That is what the social security review is all about.
We recently received a rather extensive document regarding the whole problem of social security review. I know that hon. members are very interested in suggestions put forward by the federal government. I am told that the provinces in general are very co-operative. On the other hand, it is the ability to pay for, not the desire to offer this pension that is the biggest issue. If this government spends too much, the opposition criticizes us for over-spending. We are criticized for our priorities.
Here we are establishing a priority. We said the Canada Pension Plan will be enlarged to include the spouse. In spite of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, I find this a very progressive move. It will possibly be studied in committee soon and, I hope, come into effect in October 1975.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF FULL-TIME MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief tonight. I should like to leave one thought with the House on third reading. At the outset, I
Law Reform Commission Act
should like to say that every member of the House of Commons, every lawyer, anyhow, supports the idea of the Law Reform Commission and its work. To illustrate the difficulty of the field in which it is engaged, perhaps I might be allowed to quote from a Russian philosopher. Speaking about the problem of segregating the good from the bad, he had this to say:
Let the reader who expects this book to be a political expose slam its covers shut right now. If only it were so simple! If only there were people somewhere insidiously committing evil deeds and it were necessary only to separate them from the rest of us and destroy them. But the line dividing good and evil cuts through the heart of every human being. And who is willing to destroy a piece of his own heart?
During the life of any heart this line keeps changing place. Sometimes it is squeezed one way by exuberant evil and sometimes it shifts to allow enough space for good to flourish. One and the same human being is, at various ages, under various circumstances, a totally different human being. At times he is close to being a devil, at times to sainthood. But his name doesn't change and to that name we ascribe the whole lot, good and evil.
I understand well the functions of the Law Reform Commission and I have just done some research on the various reports the Commission has brought out. Up to this point, the Commission has been engaged, it seems to me, in a philosophic approach. On the practical side it has been dealing with the reform of our correctional institutions, and so on. However, it is time, now, for the Law Reform Commission, this parliament and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) in particular to examine the Criminal Code carefully with a view to making necessary changes. I am speaking from memory, but I believe it was Stevens of England who put the Code together in 1887 and except for a few changes it was adopted by Canada in the early 1900's-1906 to be exact. Since then, some changes have been made but there are still sections of it which provide, for example, for a person seven years and older being charged with a criminal offence in certain circumstances; there are still sections dealing with insanity which are more than 100 years old.
This is, of course, International Women's Year the theme of which is equality for the other sex, a concept I certainly endorse. There are certain sections dealing with certain offences; if a male is a certain age and the female is a certain age, the male is subject to a charge of statutory rape. I have brought these sections to the attention of the minister and of the Commission. Dozens of sections are archaic and outdated; it is high time they were changed, especially in the light of the fact that the government has been returned with a big majority and with the endorsa-tion of the Canadian people. This is the time for us to get together and produce a Criminal Code adapted to the situation in 1975 rather than conditions in 1910, 1920, 1930 or even a decade ago. Let us get on with the job. Let us streamline and reform the Criminal Code to meet the changed social climate now.
It seems to me we have lost the track. All the efforts of the Law Reform Commission seem to be directed to the treatment of those who have committed violent crimes-I shall not get into that field now, because I have definite views on it. I have a great deal of respect for the Department of Justice. I think the department can be proud of its record over the years, especially when one compares it with what has been taking place in other countries, including the United States. One can be proud of the men

Grain
who work there and who have worked there over the years. The department has benefitted from the work of good scholars, many of them Rhodes scholars, conscientious workers and fine persons who really believe there should be a new national policy as far as the Criminal Code is concerned.
Having said that, and spoken for less than ten minutes, which is not long for the hon. member for Calgary North, I will simply conclude by asking the minister to get on with the job.
Motion agreed to, bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am utterly amazed that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) should quickly cry "carried" when you called this bill. The NDP have long professed to be the spokesmen for the wheat farmer of Saskatchewan. One can only assume that they sorely miss the old and tired member of the National Farmers Union who was a member of parliament for a short while; I seem to have forgotten his name but I think he was from Saskatoon-Biggar. He was old and tired, but he always tried to keep the NDP interested in the Saskatchewan farmer. If he were still here he would not have let the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre shout "carried" to a grain marketing bill at a time when the grain marketing situation in Canada is in utter chaos. Any member of the House would be derelict in his duty if he allowed the bill to pass without referring to some of the errors the government has made recently and is making today in the area of grain marketing.
Many members may wonder what Bill C-10 is all about. It is a strange piece of legislation. I well remember around 1957, 1958 or 1959 the government of the day bringing in a bill on cash advances that would allow the farmer to receive money for grain he held in storage but was unable to deliver. The amount was increased from a maximum of $3,000 to $6,000. I know inflation has had a great effect on costs, but Bill C-10 jumps the maximum from $6,000 to $15,000; and if a farmer is operating a farm in partnership with a brother, his mother, sister, or cousin he can jump the maximum to $30,000.
It has commonly been said from time to time that the right hand of government hardly knows what the left hand is doing. That has commonly been said, I suppose, of governments of yesteryear and it probably will continue to be said of governments of the future. The strange thing we see this evening is that the right hand of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board evidently does not know what the minister's left hand is doing.

The other day I read in the Globe and Mail an article which said the minister in charge of the Wheat Board was urging farmers to deliver their grain because he was concerned and worried that the Wheat Board's sales commitments would not be met. The farmers were somewhat reluctant to make deliveries of their grain, as payments had been made to them in January of 1975 on crops that were sold in the 1974 crop year. This bill, in effect, is telling the farmers: "Don't deliver your grain; take a cash advance on it up to $15,000". Did I correctly read the minister's remarks of two weeks ago when he urged farmers to make deliveries? As I say, the bill now before us does the very contrary.
The original purpose of the cash advance legislation was to give money to destitute farmers who were unable to deliver their grain. The government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced this legislation to help the farmers. The wheat farmers on the prairies today received millions of dollars in January of the current calendar year. They do not want to put themselves in a position where they pay too much income tax, so the tendency is not to deliver wheat. We are now being asked to pass a piece of legislation that will encourage them not to deliver their wheat.
According to the latest figures I have seen, there are 189 million bushels of grain and wheat in commercial storage, nearly an all-time low and the lowest amount in commercial storage in the past 20 years. It is low for two reasons. We had a poor crop last fall; the other reason is that farmers are in no rush to deliver because their cash flow position-a common expression today-is relatively good.
When this bill was considered in committee, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) said, as reported at page 10 of the committee proceedings for Tuesday, February 4, 1975:
I think the necessity for this bill-
He was merely fishing to find out just why the bill was coming forward at this time.
-sort of points up some of the real problems in our grain industry; that if delivery opportunities were available and the grain was moving continually, there would really be no need for this type of legislation.
The hon. member is really saying that, if all things were what they appeared to be, there would be no need for this type of legislation. He then asked the minister whether he agreed, and the minister replied:
No, I do not think we should ever try to build a commercial system-
The minister's motivation in this instance has to do with what is in store for the wheat farmer in the year 1975, since the railways want to abandon some 6,200 miles of track, and all the delivery points along the way. The minister's reply:
No, I do not think we should ever try to build a commercial system that can hold every bushel of grain immediately and therefore allow for the purchase of it. The quota system allows for the phasing over a year of the Wheat Board delivery opportunity, and the bill itself was particularly designed to make it even easier for those farmers who have feed grain, and who want cash, to hold and deliver later to the Canadian Wheat Board rather than be under a cash pressure to deliver it to the open market.
There are two significant points in that paragraph. First of all, the minister readily admits that, so far as commercial grain storage is concerned, we are in for a shock in
March 3, 1975

1975. They are going to be arguing whether 6,200 miles of railway track should be done away with, and a great number of delivery points may well be considered for abandonment in 1975.
The other point which is apparent in that paragraph is found in the last sentence which reads:
-the Wheat Board delivery opportunity ... was particularly designed to make it even easier for those farmers who have feed grain, and who want cash, to hold and deliver later to the Canadian Wheat Board rather than be under a cash pressure to deliver it to the open market.
The minister is concerned, as are many farmers in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and some parts of Alberta, that too much grain is being delivered on the open market and not enough consigned to the Canadian Wheat Board. We all know that the Canadian Wheat Board has made sales commitments in respect of millions of bushels for delivery later on, so the minister wants to be sure that he will have enough delivered to the Wheat Board and not too much to the open market. Those are the two significant parts, the cash advances on the grain in storage on the prairies, and the recognition of the deficiency in the system in that farmers may well sell too much on the open market so that the Wheat Board may not be able to meet its commitments later on this year to deliver the grain already sold.
There are other problems in respect of the grain industry which I think I would be remiss if I did not mention. Before getting into those problems, it is of interest to note that at the recent Agricultural Outlook Conference there were many important statements in respect of farm costs. I would be remiss if I did not point out that it is a recognized fact in the agricultural industry that costs are rising to a much greater extent than prices at this particular time.
Bill C-10 makes no mention of the amount that will be advanced on each bushel the farmer holds in storage. This is a key question. How much is the government going to allow per bushel which will allow the farmer to take up to the maximum of $15,000? Will this put the farmer in an overdraft position before the end of the year if the allowance is too great? The minister got into this trouble in the past when he first tried to amend this bill some years ago.
Let me refer to a news release from the agriculture department following the 1975 Agricultural Outlook Conference on January 20 and 21. It reads in part:
Even though we can expect gross farm receipts to go up by four per cent in 1975, net farm income may nose dive by 12 per cent;
They are being optimistic, and they take a similar viewpoint with regard to gross farm receipts being up 4 per cent. They are certainly optimistic when they suggest that net farm income will only nosedive by 12 per cent. The minister knows this, and I want the members of this House also to know at this time that net farm income may nosedive more than 12 per cent in 1975.1 suggest that if we are not very careful it will nosedive well below 12 per cent. This is obvious from a recent drop of over $1 in the international wheat price in the past three weeks.
This news release continues:
Grain
-the culprit will be input costs-
What is the minister doing about input costs? We have asked from time to time what the government is doing about inflation, and what its answer to inflation may be. What is the great Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), and I say that somewhat facetiously, doing about input costs to the agriculture industry today?

Is the minister and this government attempting to help the farmer when they allow strikes to go on and on and on, or when they deliberately interfere as they did in the grain handlers' strike on the west coast last May? This government told the grain handlers to cease all meaningful negotiations as it knew the grain companies were the culprits, and after the election it intended to make the grain companies pay. That is what the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board said. I was not in any position to judge who the culprit was, but I fully believe that meaningful negotiations between management and labour should have been allowed to continue.
Everybody in western Canada today knows who the culprit was in those negotiations. They know it was the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, that itinerant lawyer. Let any neutral person who knows nothing about wheat travel anywhere on the prairies and ask the simple question; what was the problem, and how did the government handle labour negotiations last year with the grain handlers? I am sure he will find that every man, woman and child in western Canada knows now that the

problems resulted from the interference of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board.
I have the utmost respect for the Canadian Wheat Board. The men in charge are doing the very best they can, but they are continually being interfered with by this minister for political purposes. I will have more to say about that when Bill S-6 comes before the House, because that is an example of what I have just said, that the minister is continually interfering. The $13 million demurrage charges should have been picked up by this government because this government deliberately interfered in that labour negotiation. The government destroyed meaningful negotiations for two months, from May 8 to July 8. Then, two months were added just for good measure. The government waited until sometime in September and then called Parliament to introduce a bill to suggest that the workers and the grain companies should meet, negotiate and settle. Grain was tied up for four months. It is no wonder the demurrage charges amounted to $13 million in the crop year 1973-74. There are additional freight charges totalling $1,600 million. The divisional handling charges amounted to $1,200,000. This is related directly to the interference by this minister in the grain marketing system.
Now, let me move on and bring this situation up to today's conditions. What do we have now? We have the GLT workers of the Public Service on strike. They have been on strike for 16 days. What is the situation at Vancouver? Over 40 ships are tied up at that port. Nobody seems to worry about that. The government is not appointing a mediator to deal with that problem. From time to time in this House there is a good deal of discussion about the poor in the world who are crying out for food. We have the Minister of Agriculture who goes to a conference on world population and food problems and who offers 36 million bushels of wheat. This was a great gesture. Yet there is a ship waiting in Vancouver harbour which is supposed to take five million bushels of wheat to Bangladesh. I do not have to tell members of this House how badly protein is needed in that country. This ship can carry five million bushels of grain. This ship was scheduled to dock to be loaded. We will be lucky if it is loaded in 30 days. In fact the people of Bangladesh and the western farmers will be lucky if it is loaded before the grain inspectors are back to work.
This government has not seriously concerned itself with the farmers and the delivery of their products. We can imagine the amount of the demurrage charges on a ship which can carry five million bushels of grain. That ship has been there for more than nine days and was scheduled to be loaded in four days. Once a ship is at the dock, the demurrage charges are rated according to its capacity.

The people know all about the direct interference of the minister in the grain marketing trade. He has not done them a service. In fact, he has done them a disservice. What has the minister done to correct this image he has created? He is playing a neat game of tricks. He is advertising widely throughout the Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta area saying that he will have an election in respect of an advisory body to the Canadian Wheat Board. A month ago the farmers were asking what this was all about. It became obvious that it was not an election. It was a gimmick the minister was using in an attempt to pacify the angry people in Saskatchewan and on the prairies. It is a gimmick. The President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the President of the Manitoba Wheat Pool, the President of the National Farmers Union, the President of the Alberta Wheat Pool and the President of Uni-Farm of Alberta are running. They are all running for the positions to which they were appointed. They may or may not be elected. Mr. Runciman, a knowledgeable and respected man in the grain trade offered his name in respect of the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. Does anyone in this House seriously expect that he will not win that election? He was on the appointed advisory board prior to this great charade.
The minister is attempting to improve his political health on the prairies. This is merely a charade to improve the minister's political health on the prairies. The minister has some other fences to mend which stretch back as far as that great program called LIFT, which meant lower inventory for tomorrow while to most of the farmers it meant lower cash for tomorrow. We know what happened. That was in 1969 and 1970. Some farmers were overpaid. The farmers were notified they were overpaid but the matter was dropped. Now, after July 8, they are proceeding to collect the overpayments. All of a sudden some farmers have been hit with bills which now appear to them to be bills which are three or four years old. The farmers do not think this is very fair. They thought it was a forgotten issue. The minister now, realizing he has some fence-mending to do, is attempting to do this.
This cash advance legislation which is before the House of Commons will accomplish absolutely nothing. This is a perfect example-and I shall end on this note-of good legislation passed in 1978-I hear some remark by the former President of the Treasury Board.

Did you say 1978?
March 3, 1975

Mr. Homer I said 1978 but I meant to say 1957. Thank you for correcting me. This legislation was passed in 1957 to solve a problem at that particular time. The problem of 1957 has long since disappeared. Farmers could not market their grain. Now, the minister is begging them to market their grain. What is the problem? In a speech I made before Christmas, sometime in the month of November, I showed the minister how he could encourage the farmers to market their grain. I told him that he would have difficulty in getting farmers to market their grain in the new calendar year. I advised him to bring forward a registered savings plan which would benefit the agricultural industry. The $4,000 allowed per person in any one year to go into a registered savings plan is of no benefit to farmers. It can be of tremendous benefit to the lunch pail workers, to people on salary, but it will not benefit the agricultural industry.
I advised the minister to allow the farmers of Saskatchewan to take the surplus money from their final payments on their grain and put it into a registered savings plan. I spoke of $50,000, but that may be too large an amount. Let them put more than $4,000 in a registered savings plan so that they can market their wheat without fear of paying an unduly large amount of income tax to the government in any one year. The government should allow farmers to spread their expenses over a more extended period of time. However, the minister did not pay particular attention to my advice. But the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) did. I spoke to him privately on the subject and I have learned some things about him. The Minister of Finance might have a bigger heart for the wheat farmers of Saskatchewan than the former dean of law of Saskatoon, the little boy who left the farmers of Saskatchewan because he hated agriculture. Now he has to administer a certain portion of the cash rewards for the agricultural industry. He is administering them in a picayune manner which is best described by the program LIFT, lower inventory for tomorrow. Otto needs a lift somewhere outside the House of Commons. There is no question about it.
The minister has failed to pay any attention to the demurrage charges that piled up last year and are continuing to pile up. He knows that the input costs in the agriculture industry are well over 12 per cent. In fact, in the past year they went up by nearly 14 per cent. That is the cost of goods that farmers have to buy in order to grow wheat. The minister is well aware of that, but he does not do a thing about it. He does not attempt to curb the demurrage charges. When he interferes directly in a labour strike, he should attempt to curb those costs with which the farmer will be faced in 1975.
The minister brought forward a piece of legislation which has long outlived its purpose. He said that it has two main purposes. I may be repeating myself but I want to make sure that members of the House know what the purpose of this legislation is. The minister says that about 6,000 miles of railway tracks in the prairies will be up for abandonment in 1975. There will be a great debate staged throughout the prairies regarding which sections of those railway tracks are to be abandoned. The minister knows that with the abandonment of that trackage, commercial storage will be reduced, but he says, "don't worry about it,
Grain
we will give you cash advances. Save your wheat, keep it for the wheat board." He knows also that there is a tendency on the part of some farmers who have not been as fortunate as others to sell their grain for cash on the open market, which he permitted under the feed grains proposal, and he is saying to those farmers, "don't sell on the open market, take this cash advance and eventually we will take your wheat". That is the second purpose of this legislation.
This bill will not solve the problems facing the agriculture industry in 1975. I do not agree with the minister that 6,000 miles of tracks will be abandoned in 1975. I think only a small portion of those 6,000 miles will be abandoned, and therefore I question the real need for this legislation. However, perhaps the minister wishes to take up the time of this House so that he will be able to say that he piloted six pieces of farm legislation through the House in the early part of 1975. Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) that I and other members of this party are also interested in the problems of the wheat farmer in western Canada. I, for one, enjoyed hearing the remarks he made because I think he described fairly accurately the situation as it affects farmers. I am sure that there is no one who opposes the idea of increasing the cash advance to farmers from $6,000 to $12,000, but I think that the country should pay some attention to what is happening in the grain industry and to the fact that farmers producing wheat have had only one exceptionally good year in the last ten or twelve years. Since that time farmers' incomes have decreased sharply, as the hon. member for Crowfoot said, partly because of high inputs, partly because of the changes that are taking place in the handling of grain, and also partly because of the desire of Canadian producers in other fields to handle grain.
Previously, it has been easy for farmers to maintain at least an adequate supply of wheat. Normally, at least a one year's supply of wheat was held either in the elevator or on the farms in western Canada. This amount has been earmarked for our international grain trade and has provided Canada with a reputation across the world as a country which can be relied upon to meet its commitments and is able to make large sales of wheat.
I am really concerned if, in amending this act as proposed in the legislation before us, we should not be asking ourselves why Bill C-10 is in the form in which it has been put forward, while a bill closely related to it in the same field, Bill S-6, comes from the other place. Both these bills affect payments, one deals with advance cash payments and the other one with final payments. However, both of them are related to the amount of money the farmer will obtain which he can consider as his year's income.
I think the changes that are being made in both cases are worthwhile and are certainly supported by most of the farmers. However, it is a fact, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Crowfoot, that we in this parliament have done absolutely nothing, less than nothing, in fact have been detrimental in many ways, in reducing the cost of the farmers' input as against the price that he gets for

the goods that he sells. We have done nothing about the railway system, or about the distribution system. We have done nothing in conjunction with farm organizations to improve the structure on which the farmer depends to move his grain at the right time and when he wants to move it. The farmer will have no control over the wheat in inland terminals nor, in my opinion, will the Wheat Board.
The question of labour disputes comes into this, too. In the current one I expect the cabinet will have to hold a meeting and decide whether or not they are going to pay up. Obviously, if they do not, there will not be a settlement. Any settlement will only affect a small number of people in the grain trade, namely, the inspectors on the west coast, but it will have far reaching effects and may determine whether there will be a postal strike or some other major strikes in a few weeks time.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer and the Wheat Board, as well as all those connected with the grain trade, have an interest in this matter but the government does not allow them any input, so they have no control over their own situation. I have seen the minister on television telling the farmer that he will sell all the grain he can produce this year but, Mr. Speaker, the farmer has always been hurt when he has followed the advice of the government about planting. The price of wheat dropped a dollar on the futures market in the last few weeks, so the farmer is going to be turning to the open market to sell wheat, oats, barley and feed in the hope of more stability. The farmers may not be willing, cash advance or not, to commit the same amount of wheat to the Wheat Board for sales abroad as they did previously. It depends too much on the pressures of the Chicago futures market and the ability of the purchasing countries to pay in a currency acceptable to Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is one of two which affect payments to the farmer in western Canada. He must decide whether he can trust this government to provide a lucrative external grain market or whether he will depend on the market at home, which appears to be more stable and to which he may divert some of the feed grains. If that happens, then Canada will not be meeting the commitments we have made and this will have an effect on our export markets for many years.
There are some things this government could do. It could provide some impetus, through the CDC or by putting money into some of the small farm machinery companies, to help reduce input costs. Canada produces some of the basic ingredients for fertilizer, yet the price of fertilizer is considerably higher here than it is in the United States. A lot of fertilizer is exported to the United States when it would be to our advantage to provide a wider distribution in this country at reduced prices.
We have never had as small a holdover of wheat as we appear to have now, Mr. Speaker. It has always been my hope that one day we would provide the farmer with enough stability so that we could hold over one winter's supply of wheat in storage for external markets. Wheat is a commodity that can be stored for a considerable length of time. Indeed, we had some wheat stored in fields for years.

That is the point. If we do not provide the farmer with the initiative to produce sufficient wheat to meet our commitments, somebody is going to starve- those who rely on the domestic market or the international market. We fought hard and spent a lot of money to win the markets we have. None have been acquired easily, except perhaps those in the last two or three years-they have been established by barter, by good faith and in countries to which we had to lend money. If we want the western farmer to stay in production we must provide him with the machinery that will allow him to produce for a fair and reasonable return.
Just the other day the minister suggested to farmers that instead of having the normal summer fallow they should put that land into wheat. That is a very curious thing for this minister to say. He is the one who engineered the LIFT program to take acreage out of production and put it into forage crops and summer fallow. Now, he is telling the farmers the reverse. The minister was dead wrong then, and he is probably dead wrong now. His track record has been dismal in this field as well as in other fields.
Canadians are vitally interested in seeing western grain producers lower their production costs and maintain viable operations. If prices drop, as seems very likely, and if input costs do not fall correspondingly, farmers will be in a difficult position. Farm production will not expand. It has often been said that this country can increase the production of almost any agricultural commodity, if the price is right. For the farmer the price has seldom been right; often it has been wrong.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Crowfoot suggest that the minister responsible for the Wheat Board had caused farmers to be overpaid during the election campaign and that he is trying to recover overpayments now, when farm input costs are rising and the price of produce dropping.
This bill will provide cash advances of $15,000 to the single farmer; of $30,000 to two partners who are over 18, and of $45,000 to more than two partners. But, Mr. Speaker, do not forget that money advanced must be repaid. The advance is an advance against the final amount received for production. The success of this legislation depends on the co-operation of the entire industry. It will only work if we can meet the commitments we have made, if the farmer decides not to sell on the open market and not to the feed grain industry which is offering alltime high prices for feed grains. If it does not work, the nation will suffer.
This bill will not provide the safeguards to the farmer which it should provide. It can only provide safeguards if we are willing to look at input costs of farm production and at such areas as fertilizer costs. As I said, farm production costs are rising. The farmer must worry about the weather, about grasshoppers-

Cash advances will bring advantage only if parliament stabilizes farmers' incomes. Farmers will produce more only if they can be sure of recovering at least their cost of production. They will heed government calls for increased production only if a little remains in their pockets after they have paid input costs and cash advances. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to contribute very briefly to the debate before we pass Bill C-10 providing for an increase in the payments made to prairie grain producers.
In my opinion, the inflation period we are going through will not come to an end; at least I think it will never stop by itself unless Parliament really sets its mind to check it and avoid disaster.
When the law was passed 17 or 18 years ago of course the fixed rate was then consistent with the value of the Canadian dollar. But in 1975 at a time when it is worth 44 per cent less, I do not think that to raise the advance from $6,000 to $15,000 is exaggerated. Prairie grain producers have had to invest considerably to update their equipment to be able to do their tasks at the appropriate time because of a shortage of manpower. It is not that there are not enough workers in the country, but there are not enough people interested in agriculture. Farmers must take the necessary measures to produce. They make every effort to reach their aim.
Of course, they had to borrow additional capital to buy new machinery. It takes much more income to pay the interest on those loans; finally, they end up in a difficult situation.
Agriculture is an industry with many problems. One can never depend on the stability of the industry. One year the crops will be good, the next, bad. Many factors enter the picture. There is the weather, over which one has no control. There are the markets, supply and demand, domestic and foreign markets, as many questions marks, as many causes of uncertainty. This, Mr. Speaker, applies to both eastern and western producers. The farmers must always struggle along, day after day, and ask the governments to pass laws that will ensure a certain production, a certain income, that they might be able to meet their obligations.
But what surprises me in all this, Mr. Speaker, is that during the second half of the 20th century, our problem is not that of knowing how to produce. If we let the farmers, those who are interested in farm production, do as much as they can, farm production will progress enormously. This is so true that in many areas of agriculture in our country, there are measures aimed at slowing down pro-
Grain
duction. In many areas of Canadian agriculture, there are quota systems. The bill aims at stopping production, not because too much is produced through out the world, since there obviously is not enough, but in the hope of ensuring to farm producers that their products will be sold at a price which will give them a certain income. But here again, we know that there is disorder. Some people like to play tricks and hide-and-seek. They like to misuse legislation and they do so to legislation that parliamentarians pass in good faith to protect this class of workers. We saw this again recently. I talked about it in the House today. Canada now imports poultry while it can produce sufficient quantities to meet the needs of all Canadians, and even more, since poultry producers follow a quota system. They recently had to reduce their quotas so as not to flood the market. At the same time, some people import poultry and this angers the producers. We read recently in the newspapers that poultry producers took over a truck which was bringing American chickens to a Quebec slaughterhouse. They had a barbecue in the streets while there are families in Canada, in Quebec, in every one of our cities, and even throughout the world, who could have used this food.
This is a waste. Something else could be done. We should act differently. Statistics were recently published which gave the names of those who are interested in sharing throughout the world, who know the developing countries, the under-developed countries where peoples are really in need, who do not have the food needed on a daily basis to satisfy their hunger.
It is forecasted that in 1975, 75 million people might lose their lives precisely because they will not have enough food on their table while at home we paralyze production because of domestic problems we try to solve. It is for that reason I think we should change somewhat our attitude, our approach.
The United Nations are an organization that was set up a number of years ago to promote peace in the world. It is all very fine, and I think the United Nations should continue to exist. But instead of talking only of nuclear arms, defence, wars left and right, I think the leaders could devote a little more time to examining the possibilities of different countries to bring help to underdeveloped countries, starving nations. A lot more money should be devoted to ensuring the survival of humanity instead of spending so many billions of dollars on new research, new arms in case of war. So if we want that to happen let Canada show leadership through its delegates when they meet at the United Nations. If the United States do the same we will certainly be able to find a way of having our grain distributed among the countries of the world at prices acceptable to producers. We will then stop always quarrelling on this same subject, and wondering what we are going to do with our grain, and what our producers can hope for the future.
Bill C-10 is a necessary measure because it meets a need. I urge farmers, prairie grain producers, where the land is suitable for that production, to continue to produce, do their best, do their work. For our part, this is why we are paid. We must draw up and pass the legislation to ensure the distribution of grain throughout the world. We will thus work constructively to promote peace which is

Canada has a task to fulfil. They will understand that it is possible in the twentieth century to establish lasting peace conditioned by the free circulation of goods to meet the needs of each and everyone.
