Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the debate this evening that the subject of grain is almost irresistible. As the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) pointed out, this bill is a long way down the list of priorities when one considers what is wrong with our grain industry. When I think back to the fifties, no one worked harder and wanted cash advances more than my good Liberal farmer friends. However, the Liberal government of the day said it could not be done. They said if it were ever done, it would cost the grain companies huge sums of money, the farmers would not make their payments and so on. When this legislation was first introduced, they opposed it.
It was not until a young fellow called Alvin Hamilton came along during the Diefenbaker years that we got cash advances. It is also noteworthy that during the term of that government, a no strike deal was negotiated at the Pacific seaboard. That deal lasted for a good number of years. Compare that with the present situation with strikes from one end of the country to the other. We have already lost over 80 days at Pacific seaboard because of strikes and shutdowns. There have been four separate strikes. We have no international grain agreement. We are losing sales to the United States. Japan is tendering in the market, and there were six cargoes in the last week that we should have had. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board must be about ready to announce to the world that Canada is out of the market. At the same time he could well announce to our producers that their delivery opportunities are frozen.
The situation has changed greatly in western Canada since this legislation was first introduced 17 or 18 years ago. Many farmers have to take an advance now because the trains just do not run anymore on our branch lines. This legislation can be used, in the minds of many, to coerce farmers into hauling greater distances. It seems to many producers that this is just another part of an overall plan the minister has to make changes just for the sake of change.
I hope the minister will consider some measure of compensation for the country's grain buyers who are responsible for most of the cost of administering this program

but receive nothing in return, while at the same time they are subject to some liability under it. It is not good enough for the minister to say that it is the responsibility of the companies to look after the grain buyers. The country elevator operator is the cash register of the western grain industry. It is the only business I know where one man's signature on a cheque can commit his company to hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. I really believe the country grain buyer deserves a better shake from the government.
The minister, in closing the debate on second reading, did his best to indicate the prosperity of western farmers, quoting figures to prove that the average net farm income for 1974 would be over $23,000 per farmer. I leave it to the farmers of western Canada to judge the accuracy of those figures.

Now, I want to read another significant statement which appears in the same paragraph. The minister added:
It is almost impossible for the Canadian Wheat Board to make a payment before January 1.
Let us analyze those words. Let us cast our minds back. In what year in the recent past, was there a payment made before January 1? Scratch our heads. Everybody thinks: My, it was the year 1972 when there was an election on October 30. That was the year in which the minister did the impossible.

Someone said "forked tongue". He had a tongue that spoke one way in one part of Canada and another way in another part of the country.
As I say, this is an interesting paragraph. I have not got to the end of it yet. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board went on to say this:
As the present law stands, if the board can close its pool and therefore be ready to make a payment, it has to make the payment. In at least one recent year, this meant that the payment came rather unexpectedly to tax planning farmers in December.
He admits it was one recent year. The tax planning farmers had nothing to do with it. Vote-gathering Liberals offered the payment to the farmers on October 15, 1972 and the Wheat Board was then obliged to go ahead and make payment. The payment arrived in the hands of the tax planning farmers in December. Talk about a con game!
This is the Senate taking a hand in the operations of government. This is one of the most commendable pieces of legislation the Senate has sent to us in years. If we go back to 1867, we find the Senate is supposed-it does not,
Grain
but it is supposed-to act in a non-partisan manner, for the good of the country and not for the good of a political party. The Senate is slapping the wrist of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and is saying: "No more abuses; no more direct interference with the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board." The Canadian Wheat Board operates for the good of the Canadian wheat farmer, not for the good of the political party which happens to be in power at any given time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: Or for the good of the opposition.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
I hear an hon. member standing behind the curtain making a comment. If he wants to make a speech on this bill, I will spare him some time before ten o'clock if he comes forward. In any event, the significant thing that we are witnessing here tonight is that the Senate is slapping the wrist of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and saying there will be no more interference with the Canadian Wheat Board, no more of this trick of using the farmers' own money to buy votes.
Most members of the House of Commons think that final payments on wheat come from the general treasury. We are not dealing here with some kind of subsidy out of general revenue; we are dealing with the farmers' own money which accumulates in the pool accounts of the Canadian Wheat Board and is paid to the farmers when the Wheat Board settles those accounts. The minister's own admission on page 6 of the committee report is that this payment was made unexpectedly in only one year, and that it is almost impossible for the Canadian Wheat Board to settle accounts before January 1.
All hon. members know the job of the Canadian Wheat Board is to sell wheat for the Canadian farmer. It does the Canadian farmer a disservice if some elected official superimposes his wish upon the board's and tells them to stop selling wheat and to total up their accounts, because he is in political trouble and wants to offer the farmer some money. On that particular occasion the Conservative party, which happened to be the official opposition, had some very knowledgeable members in the wheat trade. They did the best calculations they could and decided that the pool accounts could safely be offered an additional 25 cents, and as an official policy they proposed a 25 cent boost in the initial price of wheat. This offer came out some time in September. I am pointing this out so the House can fully realize that the minister knew exactly what he was doing when he did the impossible in 1972. The official opposition said that the initial price was too low, that if they had been the government they would have increased the initial price by 25 cents a bushel at the beginning of the crop year on August 1.
I well remember the minister's initial reaction. He scoffed at that offer in his arrogant way and said we were insulting the knowledge of the farmers. Then, as the campaign wore on, he realized that the farmers had accepted the proposition that the initial price should be 25 cents a bushel higher than it was, so he directly interfered with the Canadian Wheat Board and told them he was going to make another offer. He said: "We have an election; we have to buy votes with the farmers' own money", and so he made an offer of 30 cents.

'	Grain
I have often wondered, if the official opposition at that time, figuring things out to the best of their ability, had decided that the farmers should be paid another 35 cents a bushel, whether the minister would have offered 40 cents. I have come to the conclusion that that is the way the minister reached his 30 cents. If we had offered 35 cents, he would have offered 40 cents. It was an option with the farmers' own money.
In the fall of 1972 the price of grain was not as high as it has been in the last couple of years. This was a year or two following the implementation of the LIFT program which penalized the farmers if they grew wheat. That was a time when the farmers were in need of cash. We in the opposition recognized the fact that international grain prices were going to go up. They started to go up in May 1972, and the minister made his last big sale to China in April at a very low price compared with the prices that followed. That is when he offered the farmers 30 cents, as he admitted in the committee proceedings.
Further on in the committee proceedings the minister admitted that the Wheat Board really preferred this bill. It is not a question of the minister preferring the bill but of the Wheat Board preferring the bill. I ask, why did the Wheat Board prefer this bill? Why did the bill originate in the Senate? Who in the Senate had some knowledge of the Wheat Board? The former chief commissioner who operated and managed the Wheat Board for the farmers was a member of the Senate. The minister admitted in the committee that the Wheat Board preferred this bill because then no future minister could deliberately interfere with the Wheat Board's operations for political reasons, as this minister did in 1972.
Obviously, the bill originated in the Senate because the former chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board desired something like this to protect the Wheat Board and its pool accounting system. Senator McDonald of southern Saskatchewan was a wheat farmer fully knowledgeable of the political abuses that can be perpetrated upon the wheat farmer by a Liberal government, particularly the one of Jimmy Gardiner. I would also be remiss if I did not mention the Hon. Senator Argue, a knowledgeable critic-that is the best compliment I can pay him- who is fully aware of what political implications can spell for Saskatchewan farmers from time to time.
I have no doubt that when the Wheat Board requested this bill they did not get a favourable response from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. The minister knew he was the culprit who had interfered with the Wheat Board previously. I can quite imagine that he said: "This is a minor bill; don't trouble me with it". They went to the Senate and found there a ready ally in the former chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, as well as ready support from the former member for Assiniboia, Senator Argue.
As I have said, the Canadian Wheat Board works for the wheat farmer, not for the political party in power. While the Wheat Board commissioners may be appointed by the government in power, they are to act in a non-partisan manner. Supposedly we are to gain something from this election charade the minister is carrying out in respect of advisers to the Canadian Wheat Board. One can only gather that the one little benefit to come from that is that,

over the years, it may tend to make the Wheat Board more independent of the government and more answerable to the farmers, particularly if the farmers elect the advisory committee to the Wheat Board rather than the members being appointed by the government. That is the one benefit that will come from this election charade the minister is perpetrating upon the wheat farmer. In years to come this may be a beneficial thing. The one thing which may be of benefit to the farmer is that this bill will make the Wheat Board one teeny-weeny bit more independent and protected from government interference.
If I have left no other message with members of this House tonight regarding this small, teeny-weeny bill, S-6, let me point out that the purpose is to slap the hands or the wrists of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. The reason this bill comes from the Senate is that those gentlemen there who have some knowledge about the grain trade realize the importance of the independence of the Wheat Board and that it must be maintained free of political interference. This minister has interfered with the Wheat Board for political reasons, and let there be no doubt about that. Let it long be remembered as a lesson to future ministers.
It is fine to interfere with the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board if you are pushing and promoting sales, or guaranteeing credit, as did a former minister, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), when wheat was hard to move. That is the kind of assistance the government can give. It should assist in making sales, but it should not deliberately interfere for political gain with this independent body set up to serve the farmers of western Canada. That should be a no, no, and Bill S-6 should make that abundantly clear to every member of this House of Commons.
Let me end on this note. At page 6 of the Committee's proceedings No. 18 the minister admits that the one purpose of this bill is to make certain of the year in which the final payment will be made. The minister admits, as do members of the Wheat Board, that it is almost impossible to make the final payment at any time before January 1. If this bill passes it will make it impossible, although I would not trust this minister even though he is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). I would not suggest that he would break the law, but he may well go around it as he has tried to do in the last couple of years, and as he tried to do in respect of that famous stabilization bill. I am going back to 1971, November of that year, when the minister was called before the courts just before a by-election took place in southern Saskatchewan, and he had to drop his stabilization bill. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) admitted that they were trying to go around the law, but the government hoped to change the law after it had gone around it. That is really what he said.
If this bill passes it will be impossible for any responsible minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to make the final payment before January 1. I would not say that about the present government and this minister, because this minister has accomplished the impossible in the past and he may attempt to do so in the future, but we will be on guard.

That is the recollection I have, but I am willing to correct the record if that is not the case. I will look it up tomorrow. I can recall very well the minister making an announcement during that campaign, about two weeks before the election, that the final payment would be made in that year.
This has very often been used as an election promise. That has often been done by the Liberal party in the past. I remember one member of my own constituency, the hon. Jimmy Gardiner, who used to do things like this during an election year. He used to do it very often. This was part of a great election campaign type of patronage program the Liberal party used all the time. I hope that tactics like timing the final payment on grain according to the political whims of political parties is a thing of the past. I think things of this sort explain why the Liberal party is almost irrelevant right across western Canada today, keeping in
Grain
mind the four provincial governments we have in the west.
All this bill will do is determine that the final payment will be made not sooner than January 1 of each calendar year. This will give farmers more economic stability. They will know when to expect the final payment, and will know what earnings to base their income tax on for one particular year.
As we all know, the farmer is up against all kinds of uncertainties. As suggested earlier by some hon. members, the farmer is up against uncertainties as to weather, international sales, grasshoppers and other kinds of insects, and the government in terms of its policy. This bill is one small step toward providing the farmer with some rationale on which to plan. This will give him some kind of consistency in respect of the income he is to derive.
It is very interesting to note that this bill originated in the Senate. I do not think that is a good precedent. I do not like to see bills originate in a Chamber which does not have democratically elected members. In any event, this bill did originate in the Senate and I wonder whether some of the senators really felt they could not trust the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and wanted to make sure that he was not able to play politics with the farmers' money.
It was very difficult for the farmers under the old system to know just where they were economically, because in that situation they could receive two final payments in one year. They could receive a final payment for the year just before the turn of the year, and another final payment for the previous year just after January 1. This kind of political game and this kind of inconsistency will be eliminated by Bill S-6. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, you could still have a lot of inconsistencies with the bill now before us. It does not say the money has to be paid before a certain time. It just says the final payment must be made after January 1 in each calendar year. I suppose if it were politically expedient to withhold the final payment until May or June the minister could still do that. I think this feature of the bill could be tightened up.
In any event, I think this bill is a step in the right direction. It is one very small bill which all of us in this House can support as something that should have been in force years ago. As I said, the bill originated in the Senate. I think one of the senators over there who has a bit of life and spunk decided he did not trust the Minister of Justice. Perhaps this is why the minister treats the bill so lightly. The senator introduced the legislation so the minister could not play politics with the farmers' money as he has done in the past. This is money that comes out of the final payment, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) knows. I am sure he would not play games of this sort with the farmers' money. It is the farmers' money and the farmers should not have to see that fund being used as part of a political poker game. I know the Minister of Agriculture would not do that, but the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is a different sort of politician from the congenial Minister of Agriculture. I see the Minister of Agriculture nodding his head indicating that he is in accord with me. I know he is very happy to see this bill before the House. I know that deep down in his heart he knows that this bill is a little bit of a rap on the knuckles

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this bill I must say that if there is one thing this bill does it is that it shows the lack of imagination of the government, since it must rely on the Senate to bring in the rules of application which this minister and the department he represents do not seem able to draft. One very important point should be brought to the attention of the minister. A great many farmers received two payments in one year and therefore have suffered a hardship in respect of income tax. Producers have come to me and have asked if there was something I could do for them in respect of this payment because they had actually planned their income so that they would receive that payment the following January. It had been done that way for years, but all of a sudden because there was an election there had to be a promise of a payment.
One thing the minister does not understand is the fact that one cannot buy the respect of the prairie grain producer. That election proved that. Fewer Liberals came from western Canada after the election in 1972 than before, primarily because of the fact that the western grain producer will not be bought. I presume this has been a lesson to the minister. No doubt whenever members of the Senate go to the areas they represent they find this to be a fact and, while the Senate has a vast majority of Liberal supporters and past Liberal members of parliament, I presume the Senators are trying to protect the Liberal image by not allowing the minister to do this in future.
This is what this bill is all about. It limits the period in which the minister can do this type of thing. There are many occasions when, if the minister did not interfere with the Canadian Wheat Board, the initial payments could be much higher and much closer to the final payment. It is absolutely unnecessary for an amount of 30 cents, 40 cents, 50 cents or $1 a bushel to be retained in any fund as has been the situation in some cases. When the minister interferes to keep the initial payment down and there comes a point in time when he feels he must buy the affection of the producer, he will announce an interim payment if he is permitted to do so. This is a very despicable practice in the minds of the prairie grain producers. They do not like this and, as I pointed out earlier, they will not be bought. The minister must recognize this. We

all should realize that no one is able to buy the allegiance or support of these people. While the Senate apparently sees this and tries to protect the government, we are not really sure that the minister recognizes this as a fact.
We on this side of the House have at times thought the minister had learned a lesson in certain cases but we are never actually sure that we can trust him. Regardless of how we may feel about the Senate, I suppose we must accept the fact that there comes a point in time when something good comes out of it, even though it may be a bill of little significance. Mr. Speaker, I see it is now almost ten o'clock. It is our intention to allow this bill to pass tonight. With those few remarks I am prepared to end this debate.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-LAYOFFS IN SAINT-HYACINTHE DUE TO IMPORTATIONS
INDUSTRY-LAYOFFS IN SAINT-HYACINTHE DUE TO IMPORTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in these days of stagflation where social chaos is at our doors, how can we decently, as a Parliament, allow an industry deeply rooted for decades in an area and elsewhere in the country to close down, out of a sudden, three of its divisions, and thereby deprive of their livelihood some 200 workers, men and women, without stepping in or at least raise pertinent questions?
This is the basic question facing us tonight and that 1 put to everyone here.
On February 14, Penman's Limited of Saint-Hyacinthe informed me, through their president Mr. A. P. Earle, that following the strike extant since June 10, 1974, and the subsequent losses in markets, it had regretfully decided it was not possible to reopen if and when the labor strife was settled, its spinning, felting and dyeing shops.
This would mean, Mr. Speaker, a reduction in labour force from 369 to 150, with a resulting loss of some 200 jobs.
On Friday February 28, I gladly met in Saint-Hyacinthe representatives of the workers involved, at their request. I saw there justified amazement, and even exasperation at that decision by the employer.
Most important, I felt that this new situation, arising in the middle of a conflict already nine months old, will preclude negotiations of a return-to-work agreement, since the National Knitting Union still insists on negotiating for the total number of employees, while the employer only wants to negotiate for the 150 employees present market conditions would allow him to reenlist. It can already be seen that the situation is explosive at Penman's Limited in Saint-Hyacinthe.
Are we going to go through a new Lapalme affair, mutatis mutandis? I hope not, I hope all parties concerned will think only in terms of job security for all workers involved.
Adjournment Debate
Let us be fair: the company says it deplores the effects of its decision. In addition, it is seeking the co-operation of the union, federal and provincial government agencies to appoint, jointly, a committee whose task would be to reintegrate into the labour force the largest possible number of those who have been laid off, while promising to give priority to older employees who might otherwise find it difficult if not impossible to find jobs elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, that initiative is sincere, provided of course the company, Penman's Limited at Saint-Hyacinthe as well as its parent company Dominion Textiles Limited are really wallfighting with its back to the wall, that it has not operated profitably in the last few years, nor invested abroad, either in Japan or elsewhere, amounts of money amassed here, or finally that it has not benefited from exports. Those are as many questions to which I should doubtless get replies from the company concerned any day now.
For the time being, however, I refuse to resign myself to the decision of the company, Penman's Limited. With several persons concerned, I fail to understand how the present strike at Saint-Hyacinthe could have harmed Penman's situation in the marketplace to the extent where it cannot even consider a gradual return to a normal situation, both in the market and consequently with gradual reemployment of its labour force. I request that the political authorities, federal as well as Quebec, authorities in the field of industry, trade and commerce or possibly manpower, should discuss the company's attitude before doing anything about it.
As people in my constituency said, when shall we have governments bold enough to talk to multinational or other companies? When shall we have governments which are shocked by the employment insecurity of our poor taxpayers?
It remains nevertheless-and Penman's rightly say so- that the sharp increase in imports on the main markets served by the company had a decisive influence on the announcement mode by Penman's that some 200 employees would be laid off in Saint-Hyacinthe.
Because of their lack of initiative, their lack of concern, and the excessive delay in dealing with this matter, the present government, and most of all the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), are responsible for the present textile situation in Canada and to a great extent for the layoffs in that area, and will bear the responsibility of the social chaos which might unfortunately ensue.
The minister should make a statement without delay committing the government to further restrict textile imports. The employment security of tens of thousands Canadian workers, and more particularly, on a very shortterm basis, the linelihood of some 200 Saint-Hyacinthe workers and the social order in Saint-Hyacinthe and the surrounding area are at stake.
Any ambiguous attitude on the part of the government in this matter will only make corporations like Penman's Ltd. more reluctant to carry on their operations with their full present staff.
In another respect, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) together with

Adjournment Debate
his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), and their provincial counterparts, will have to consider the opportunity of capital investments to help those industries in their updating process to keep abreast of new market needs.
Let me warn them though: such subsidies, whether under the form of loans or something else, should only be granted to factories provided it has been ascertained that they will generate more employment security and possibly more employment opportunities.
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, the Government should assure that people of Saint-Hyacinthe and especially the workers of Penman's Ltd., that every attempt possible will be made on a short term as well as on a long term basis in order to help Penman's Ltd. regain its share of the market and to help workers get back to work on a gradual basis.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the clearsightedness and solidarity of the workers involved as well as to the social conscience of the employer who has always had the benefit of a stable, competent and reasonable manpower in Saint-Hyacinthe, to settle this matter to the advantage of all parties involved, all workers involved and their families, and to the advantage of the whole community of Saint-Hyacinthe which is plagued with the repercussions of that serious problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-LAYOFFS IN SAINT-HYACINTHE DUE TO IMPORTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recommendations of the Textile and Clothing Board being examined by the government do not include the items mentioned by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, which were sweaters, T-shirts and underwear.
When representatives of the workers and the textile industry met the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) last November, they did not identify the items mentioned as being priority problems and did not ask that the Textile and Clothing Board undertake the study of these products on an urgent basis.
Moreover, we understand that the layoffs in the Penman's Ltd. plant in Saint-Hyacinthe are the result of a decision made by this company to stop manufacturing products other than sweaters, T-shirts and underwear. Therefore, we can conclude that the importation of these products is not directly responsible for the layoffs.
According to our textile policy, when a Canadian textile manufacturer believes that his business is being caused a prejudice because of importation, this manufacturer can go to the Textile and Clothing Board or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and ask for an investigation to determine if there is in fact a prejudice. Penman's did not approach the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the Textile and Clothing Board.
The government cannot be expected to act in the case of a specific company when this company sees no need to use the measures at its disposal.
However, if Penman's decides to resume manufacturing the discontinued items, I can assure the House that all appropriate programs under the jurisdiction of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be placed at its disposal.
I am certain that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Manpower

and Immigration (Mr. Andras) would say the same thing about their department.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STOPPAGE OF GRAIN SHIPMENTS BY STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP
PUBLIC SERVICE-STOPPAGE OF GRAIN SHIPMENTS BY STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to speak about the complete stoppage of shipments of all commodities from the west coast of British Columbia. I mention all commodities because on Saturday the longshoremen and warehousemen's union began a legal strike. Some time before then, the grain weighmen, public servants of Canada, went on strike legally, affecting grain shipments from the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. It might interest the House to know that between October 1, 1974 and the end of February it was impossible, for about 70 days, to ship grain from Vancouver or from the west coast generally.
These difficulties arose as a direct result of labour disputes. First, we had the grain handlers legal strike which, after stopping the flow of grain to customers abroad for many weeks, was settled by parliament with the introduction of compulsory return to work legislation on October 11, 1974. Subsequently, we had grain inspectors, who are employees of the government, booking off sick and then beginning an official strike on November 23. It lasted several weeks. Then, beginning on February 17, grain weighmen, who are public servants of Canada, went on strike with fellow workmen operating in other trades. That strike is still continuing. As I said, on Saturday, as a consequence of the legal strike of the longshoremen, the whole of the west coast is tied up and shipments are neither coming in nor going out.
The question we must consider is twofold. First, are these work stoppages affecting the national interest; second, what is the government going to do about them? This government is on record as stating its concern for the public interest when labour-management disputes arise. On February 10 the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacGuigan) said, as recorded on page 3098 of Hansard:
[DOT] .. this government has always asserted the rule of the public interest in labour disputes and has never pretended that labour disputes are matters which affect exclusively the parties.
This view was put even more forcefully on August 31, 1972, by the then minister of labour. Speaking about the longshoremen's strike then in process on the west coast, he said, as recorded on page 3901 of Hansard:
... there are occasions when parliament must deal with situations, when the full resort to economic warfare by strike or lockout so impairs the ability of others to carry on their activities that it can be said to be against the national interest for the work stoppage to continue. Parliament in this case was recalled as a last resort when it was evident that the ports on the west coast would not resume operations for some weeks if normal collective bargaining procedures were allowed to take their course.
He went on to say, as recorded on page 3902:
By far and away the hardest hit at this time is the grain economy on its external markets. This important sector of the economy is presently in the greatest jeopardy should the ports remain closed. British Columbia, too, has an export-oriented economy, and it is of the utmost importance that there be no prolonged closure of its ports.

Further, at the time of the legislation, which was introduced to end the grain handlers' strike in October 1974, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) said, and I quote from page 165 of Hansard for October 7, 1974:
The only responsible view for the government to take was that a work stoppage was not only unnecessary, in view of the existence of a reasonable and viable alternative in the form of Dr. Perry's report, but would certainly adversely affect the national interest.
He stated that in May the government had invoked Section 181 of the Canada Labour Code because any work stoppage would affect the national interest. He went on to say, and I quote:
-I think, a sufficient chronological backdrop to a situation that can no longer be allowed to run its harmful and protracted course unchecked.
On Wednesday last, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart) asked the Minister of Justice what was going to be done about the situation on the west coast. The minister's reply, which is recorded at page 3600 of Hansard for February 26, is as follows:
Mr. Speaker, a number of plans are being looked at, both in connection with the immediate period and also in connection with an attempt to catch up as quickly as possible when conditions return to normal.
The situation is certainly not returning to normal. I personally regret the fact that this government has chosen to hold the line against inflation by putting the burden on the backs of the public service workers out on strike, especially in view of the fact they are the lowest paid people in the civil service and, for that matter, in the country. I am not about to decide who is wrong in the dispute, but the longshoremen are not the lowest paid people in the country by a long shot. The dispute between the longshoremen and their employer seems to centre around the fact there is dispute over a clause which management wants to have changed. It would change the procedure for handling container cargo.
The whole of the west coast is now tied up in two disputes. The government is on record as saying on more than one occasion that its concern is the public interest. However, I asked a question of the government House leader on February 28, as recorded at page 3663 of Hansard. I quote:
-will the government House leader advise this House whether in the view of the government the national interest is being affected by the present stoppage of grain shipments due to the present legal strike?
The minister replied:
-I support the position of my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, that this is a time for negotiation-
As I said, my question is twofold.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STOPPAGE OF GRAIN SHIPMENTS BY STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time, the movement of export grain and other goods from west coast ports is being interrupted by two work stoppages, one in the public sector and one in the private sector. These groups include a walkout of the federal government's general labour and trades group, which includes grain weighmen and samplers under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Grain Commission, as well as
Adjournment Debate
approximately 4,000 longshoremen. These longshoremen have been in negotiation with the British Columbia Maritime Employers' Association and struck this past weekend in support of their demands. In this complex situation both disputes will have to be resolved before grain and other goods start moving once again. It is our hope they can be settled by a process of negotiation between the parties concerned.
While it is true that legislation has been used in the past to end disputes such as these, it is premature to suggest that this course of action will be followed, particularly since the longshoremen commenced their walk-out only today. In May of last year, after Parliament had been dissolved, the Canada Labour Code was used to prevent a work stoppage of grain elevator employees. Dissolution is not a factor this time, so the procedure under that act cannot be applied in the same manner. However, the full parliamentary process could be invoked at short notice should it be considered appropriate.
At the moment approximately 30 vessels are waiting in Vancouver to take on grain. There are almost 11,000 railway cars loaded with grain, stacked up from Vancouver and Prince Rupert back to the prairies awaiting movement.
There is no doubt these strikes are affecting a vital national interest. It is just as vital that the parties concerned, including the government, be given the opportunity of negotiating their respective positions before that right is removed by parliament.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED DELAY IN ESTABLISHING BROADCASTING STATION FOR OKANAGAN VALLEY
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED DELAY IN ESTABLISHING BROADCASTING STATION FOR OKANAGAN VALLEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, February 28, I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) whether the proposed CBC radio broadcasting station for the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia is being held up because a suitable site is being sought for a French television station. It appears that as soon as anyone asks a question in this House relating to a subject such as this he is immediately labelled antiFrench, but this is not the case. I believe this is a very legitimate question to be asking at this time.
The people of the Okanagan Valley have been asking for a CBC radio broadcasting station for a number of years. In the two and a half years that I have been here I have had a number of representations on this subject and I have discussed it with many people in the Okanagan Valley. They feel they have been discriminated against for many years by not being able to have a full CBC radio station. The proposed CBC radio station would serve about 150,000 people in the area, many of whom have moved in to retire from other areas of Canada and have had access to CBC radio. They just cannot understand why there is not a broadcasting station in the Okanagan when they move in, especially when there are so many people in the coverage area.
I have been pressing the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) and the Secretary of State over the past
i

Adjournment Debate
two years. Finally, on November 25, I received a letter from the Secretary of State in which he said:
I am advised by the CBC that barring further capital budget restraints, under the affiliate replacement plan, which applies in the case of Penticton, Kelowna and Vernon, B.C., they expect to submit an application to CRTC by the fall of 1975. The Corporation further informs me that having received CRTC approval they will need some twelve months before becoming operational in the areas you have identified.
This was very encouraging because I thought that it would bring the CBC broadcasting station quite soon to the Okanagan Valley. I also know that the existing broadcasting stations in Kelowna, Vernon and Penticton are very interested in having CBC establish a full time broadcasting station. They are so interested that they have between them devised a plan so that they would be able to accommodate a CBC radio station. This would provide the necessary engineering and funding to make available a full time radio station. The only thing they want in return is a guaranteed lease for the next few years.
I understand that this proposition has been submitted to CRTC complete with the overall monthly or yearly cost. The cost seems quite reasonable for the number of people who would be served. This service could begin very quickly, using the facilities proposed by these radio broadcasting companies. I have just recently heard that the CRTC is looking for a site in the Okanagan that would accommodate both a CBC broadcasting station and a French TV broadcasting station. It would appear that this would be a much more costly venture and would take much longer to bring into effect. The French TV station would accommodate between one and one-half per cent of the people of the Okanagan, while the CBC radio broadcasting station would accommodate over 150,000 people.
I think it would be fair to point out at this time that there are areas in my riding of Okanagan Boundary that do not even have a CBC-TV broadcasting station now, or can only receive Canadian TV through their own ingenuity, the people in the area having put up the necessary equipment themselves in order to receive this TV. I would also like to point out that there are areas in my riding that do not even get any TV, places such as Christina Lake.
I certainly believe that the majority should be serviced first by the CBC and CRTC before any moneys are spent on a costly French TV network. I would, therefore, respectfully ask that the government adopt a policy that will ensure that the majority of the people get the service
for which they have been asking and to which they should be entitled.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gustave Blouin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED DELAY IN ESTABLISHING BROADCASTING STATION FOR OKANAGAN VALLEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) I have some information obtained from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation through the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner).
Two major undertakings by the CBC are involved in the matter of improving service to the Okanagan valley. One plan is known as the radio replacement plan and the other is known as the accelerated coverage plan. The radio replacement plan arises out of the fact that many years ago resources were not available for the CBC to build its own radio transmitters in many locations. The private sector of radio was, therefore, given the responsibility of representing the CBC in many communities. The privately owned stations could carry only a portion of the total service, but this was better than no service at all.
In recent years commercial radio network programming has dropped markedly and radio broadcasting styles have changed; the affiliation arrangements in radio have become more and more unsatisfactory to both the CBC and the privately owned radio affiliates. As a consequence, the CBC has recently embarked on a program of construction of its own radio transmitters in order to eliminate to a great extent the need for affiliation. Three such transmitters, broadcasting the complete CBC English AM radio network service, are planned for Kelowna, Penticton and Vernon. In addition, Kamloops forms part of this group.
Early last year the CBC had hoped to apply for licences for those three stations late in 1974. The effect of inflation on the CBC's capital budget has caused a postponement of the licence applications, and it is now expected that the applications will be submitted late this year.
The other major CBC undertaking is the accelerated coverage plan. Under this plan, CBC service will be extended in the required official language to all unserved areas containing 500 or more people. Under this plan, French service will be extended to Kelowna in late 1977. The CBC wishes to make clear that the accelerated coverage plan is separately funded; the accelerated coverage plan is not responsible for the budget constraints experienced by the CBC's radio replacement plan, and the resultant one year delay in the plans for CBC English language radio transmitters in Kelowna, Penticton and Vernon, together with Kamloops.
